articles.title: Key Biden aide Brett McGurk on Hamas, Iran, Saudi Arabia and why U.S. nearly took "draconian measures" against Israel - CBS News
articles.summary: Key Biden aide Brett McGurk on Hamas, Iran, Saudi Arabia and why U.S. nearly took "draconian measures" against Israel  CBS News‘Ready to Blow His Stack’: How Biden Nearly Cut Off Netanyahu Over Gaza  nytimes.comBiden Reportedly Considered Cutting Arms to Israel  YahooHow Biden Averted a War With Iran  The AtlanticTranscript: Brett McGurk on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," Oct. 4, 2026  CBS News
articles.full_text:
President Joe Biden was on the verge of taking "draconian measures" after an Israeli military drone strike killed in the Gaza Strip in April 2024, but U.S. intelligence that Iran was about to launch an "unprecedented" prevented Biden from moving forward, according to Brett McGurk, a top Middle East adviser to four presidents.
In an interview with "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" taped Thursday, McGurk described Biden as "fed up" with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's handling of the war in Gaza.
"At that moment, if not for that impending missile attack, which we then had to deploy military forces … I think we would have taken some pretty draconian measures against Israel," he said, adding that cutting off U.S. weapons to Israel "was very much on the table."
The U.S. and its Arab and European partners helped protect Israel from the Iranian attack, which McGurk said included 120 ballistic missiles, 170 drones and 30 cruise missiles that were "all launched to land at the same time."
In his new memoir titled "Brink," which is set to be published Tuesday, McGurk recalled a tense conversation between Biden and Netanyahu around that time in which the U.S. leader warned the prime minister he could end the weapons supply. At the time, the Israeli government said it believed there were more than 130 hostages in Gaza and around 34,000 Gazan deaths, according to the Hamas-run Gaza Ministry of Health.
"You think I'm Santa Claus? No Santa in Israel, pal," McGurk quotes Biden as saying.
In McGurk's interview with CBS News, the longtime foreign policy aide recounted the Biden administration's initial reaction to Hamas' Oct. 7 terror attack on Israel, its handling of Israel's war against Hamas in Gaza, the efforts to secure an Israel-Hamas ceasefire and hostage release deal, the role of Iran and — starting years earlier — a long-sought push to normalize relations between Israel and Saudi Arabia.
McGurk is no longer working with the Bidens and is currently a CNN contributor.
McGurk: "If you just stop American support for Israel, that is not going to end the crisis"
Biden's handling of the Israel-Hamas war has drawn years of scrutiny — including from within his own party. During the 2024 presidential campaign, the administration faced to stop military aid to Israel amid the humanitarian crisis in Gaza.
The U.S. is the largest weapons supplier to Israel, and provides billions in aid. A of Israel's conduct found that it was "reasonable to assess" that Israeli security forces have used U.S.-made weapons in ways "inconsistent with" international humanitarian law obligations. Casualties in Gaza, "including high levels of civilian casualties," raised "substantial questions as to whether the IDF is using" U.S.-made weapons "effectively in all cases," the report said.
Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen in November 2024 that Biden didn't use U.S. leverage effectively, arguing he sent Israel "more bombs and more money" after Netaynahu disregarded his requests, and pointed to U.S. laws blocking arms shipments to military units that violated human rights.
Since then, debates over the future of U.S.-Israel relations have . Some of the criticism that the Biden administration was not strong enough in its response to Israeli actions in Gaza has been directed at McGurk, who was the White House National Security Council's coordinator for the Middle East and North Africa and one of his most influential advisers.
McGurk noted that the Biden administration did to Israel, including 2,000-pound bombs but never instituted a weapons halt. He believes some of the calls to go further may not have been effective.
"Israel also has one of the largest arms industries in the world, so the idea that had Biden gone further on a step on that course, it would have stopped the war, I just think the record does not support that," McGurk said.
McGurk also argued that exerting too much public pressure on Israel could have hardened Hamas' stance, ultimately setting back the negotiations to end the war in Gaza and release the hostages.
"I come back to the question: How do you end this crisis?" he said. "And I think the record shows: If you just stop American support for Israel, that is not going to end the crisis, it's going to make it worse."
At the same time as the Israel-Hamas war, attacks on U.S. forces by Iranian-backed proxy groups surged. McGurk pushed Biden to punish Iran in an effort to deter the attacks, and expressed some frustration with Biden administration colleagues who were wary of striking Iranian officials in response.
What would've happened if Iran "made a dash" toward weapons-grade uranium
McGurk said part of Biden's goal was to prevent the outbreak of a broader regional war. Meanwhile, between Iran and Israel continued.
In December 2024, McGurk traveled to Israel with national security adviser Jake Sullivan as they worked toward a deal with Hamas to release the remaining Israeli hostages.
During the visit, according to McGurk, Netanyahu talked about taking out nuclear sites in Iran, including at Fordow, a facility built inside a mountain that processed and stored highly enriched uranium. Fordow was one of the three Iranian nuclear sites that President Trump ordered to be bombed , eight months before the Trump administration and Israeli forces launched a wider war against Iran.
McGurk said the Biden administration was concerned in late 2024 that Iran "might make a dash" toward making weapons-grade uranium, and officials were open to carrying out strikes if there were evidence obtained that showed Iran was making a bomb. Netanyahu urged the US not to wait for that step. Iran had been building up a stockpile of 60%-enriched uranium, which is a short step from the material required to build a bomb.
"We actually had a principals committee meeting — that's everybody around the table — what would we do if we see that?" McGurk said. "And as I recall, unanimity on: We would do the strike in Fordow. We didn't see that. We sent a message to Iran, don't even think about it. But yet Netanyahu was clearly contemplating that."

McGurk said he and Mr. Trump's Middle East envoy Steve Witkoff "agreed we're going to work in lockstep." He described how the Biden and Trump teams put pressure on both Hamas and Israel.

U.S. saw no "warning or indicator" of Oct. 7 attack
The circumstances leading up to the Oct. 7 attack have drawn renewed attention in recent weeks, as The New York Times, The Atlantic and the Israeli newspaper Haaretz report on warnings that officials in Egypt and the United Arab Emirates allegedly delivered to Israel that Hamas was planning a major attack. Netanyahu has strongly denied that there were any warnings, but his opponents in Israel's election later this month have expressed outrage.
CBS has confirmed via a former US official and a diplomatic source that Emirati Sheikh Mohammed bin Zayed al Nahyan, President of the UAE, did share a warning with Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu in the weeks leading up to the attack. The UAE had learned that Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar was preparing a major attack but did not have specific intelligence such as a date, time or location.
McGurk told CBS News the U.S. had no intelligence that could have warned about Hamas' Oct. 7 attack.
"We did not have anything in our system that would have been a warning and indicator," he said. "No U.S. intelligence of a warning or indicator."
But he said Israel should launch an official inquiry that probes its own security establishment and political leadership, much like the U.S. did after the 9/11 attacks.
"I think they had an assumption that was deeply ingrained that Hamas was deterred, assuaged, and was not about to do something massive on any scale like this," McGurk said. "I think that was a false assumption in their system, a failure of imagination, and it was tragic."
McGurk on the Biden-MBS fist bump: "I encouraged the president to just shake his hand"
Hours before the Oct. 7 2023 attack, McGurk said he met with the Saudi Arabian Ambassador to the U.S., Princess Reema Bandar, to discuss a different issue — a potential pathway for Israel and Saudi Arabia to normalize relations.

"I believe that we are at the cusp of an even more dramatic breakthrough: an historic peace with Saudi Arabia," Netanyahu said.
The idea of Saudi Arabia establishing formal diplomatic ties with Israel had been floated to McGurk by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman nearly two years earlier, in January 2021, shortly after Biden took office, McGurk said, a deal that would have included a pathway to a Palestinian peace agreement. McGurk said he reported that extraordinary offer back to the President, but the U.S. did not act on it.
Biden was skeptical of Saudi Arabia, vowing in the 2020 Democratic primaries to treat the kingdom as a "pariah" due to U.S. intelligence indicating that Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman was linked to the murder of Washington Post columnist Jamal Khashoggi.
McGurk also explained that Biden did not want to focus on the Middle East, and only reached out to the Gulf States after the chaotic August 2021 U.S. exit from Afghanistan caused the emergency need for the U.S. to ask those governments to take in Afghan allies fleeing the Taliban. The U.S. needed another favor in 2022 when Russia invaded Ukraine, and turned again to the Gulf states, specifically Saudi Arabia, asking them to pump more oil to alleviate a spike in prices.

articles.title: 2034 World Cup: Saudi Arabia puts $2.5bn NEOM stadium on hold amid infrastructure review - Business News Nigeria
articles.summary: 2034 World Cup: Saudi Arabia puts $2.5bn NEOM stadium on hold amid infrastructure review  Business News Nigeria
articles.full_text:
Saudi Arabia has put plans for a $2.5 billion stadium intended to host matches at the 2034 FIFA World Cup on hold, as the kingdom evaluates some of its ambitious projects under its Vision 2030 economic diversification programme.
The 46,000-seat NEOM Stadium, planned as one of the tournament’s venues, is listed as on hold with no completion date in data from MEED Projects, according to Reuters. Two sources familiar with the project also said plans to build the stadium had been shelved indefinitely.
The futuristic venue was designed to be built about 350 metres above ground within The Line, a 160 kilometer steel-and-glass development that forms part of the wider NEOM project.
Saudi Arabia was officially named host of the 2034 FIFA World Cup after its bid was ratified by acclamation on December 11, 2024, at an Extraordinary FIFA Congress in Zurich, Switzerland. The kingdom was the sole bidding candidate.
Read Also: FIFA confirms Saudi Arabia as host for 2034 World Cup amid controversy
The tournament will be the third men’s FIFA World Cup hosted in the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) region, after South Korea and Japan in 2002 and Qatar in 2022. It will also be the first 48-team World Cup hosted by a single nation.
NEOM project faces reprioritisation
The decision comes as Saudi Arabia reassesses some of its largest development projects under Vision 2030, an ambitious programme aimed at diversifying the economy and reducing its dependence on oil.
Yasir Al-Rumayyan, governor of the Public Investment Fund, which owns NEOM, said in April that The Line was no longer a priority and was not essential to deliver before 2030, although he denied that projects had been cancelled.
The NEOM Stadium was originally conceived as an elevated arena within The Line and formed part of Saudi Arabia’s plans to showcase the kingdom’s futuristic infrastructure during the World Cup.
NEOM and the Saudi government’s media office did not respond to requests for comment on the stadium. Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Sports referred questions to the World Cup 2034 Hosting Higher Authority.
The authority said substantial construction milestones for the tournament were already being delivered but did not directly address the NEOM Stadium or its reported cost.
$22.7bn World Cup infrastructure programme
Saudi Arabia plans to stage the tournament across five host cities; Riyadh, Jeddah, Al Khobar, Abha and NEOM.
The kingdom plans to build or renovate 15 stadiums across the five cities, comprising 10 new venues and five major renovations, alongside major transport and infrastructure projects. MEED Projects estimates the total value of World Cup-related projects at $22.7 billion.
Despite the NEOM Stadium being put on hold, other major venues are progressing. The Prince Mohammed Bin Salman Stadium in Qiddiya, for example, has advanced with major construction and recently secured a $221 million mechanical, electrical and plumbing contract.
Saudi Arabia’s 2034 World Cup is a major component of its global sports strategy, which has seen the Public Investment Fund invest heavily in football and other sports as part of Vision 2030.
Financial and geopolitical pressures
The decision to put the NEOM Stadium on hold comes amid wider financial and geopolitical pressures facing the kingdom.
Saudi Arabia is dealing with disruptions to energy shipments and security risks linked to the regional conflict, including attacks by Iran-backed Houthi forces, while weaker oil activity has added pressure to the economy.
Reuters reported that Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Finance expects a wider fiscal deficit and a 3.6 percent contraction in real GDP this year.
The developments have increased scrutiny of the kingdom’s spending commitments under Vision 2030, particularly its large-scale giga-projects designed to transform the economy and reduce its reliance on oil.
The World Cup remains a major pillar of that strategy, with Saudi Arabia continuing to invest in football infrastructure even as some of its most ambitious development projects are delayed, downsised or reprioritised.

articles.title: Between Entrapment and Abandonment: The Mecca Pact Faces Its First Serious Test - RealClearDefense
articles.summary: Between Entrapment and Abandonment: The Mecca Pact Faces Its First Serious Test  RealClearDefenseTurkey says Mecca pact committee to meet in Riyadh on October 5  ReutersPakistan suggests talking to Houthis as Riyadh weighs military options  The Arab WeeklySaudi Arabia not to compromise on security as Houthis choose ‘chaos’: MBS  Al JazeeraAs Saudi Arabia steps up war against Houthis, Pakistan set to play support role  South China Morning Post
articles.full_text:
Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, and Türkiye made an unusually sweeping promise to one another when they signed the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement on August 7: an armed attack on one would be treated as an attack on all three. The agreement seeks to strengthen collective deterrence by confronting potential adversaries with the combined power of three of the Muslim world’s most consequential states.
Less than two months later, that promise is facing its first serious test. Houthi missiles and drones have repeatedly targeted Saudi Arabia. Pakistan has carried out air and drone strikes inside Afghanistan amid escalating cross-border violence. And Türkiye’s increasingly adversarial relationship with Israel has taken on a dangerous military dimension in Syria.
These developments expose a dilemma built into the pact from the start. Make the guarantee broad enough to deter, and the three countries risk being drawn into wars arising from threats they do not share. Limit it enough to preserve strategic autonomy, and the pact risks losing the credibility that gives collective defense its deterrent power.
Alliance theory has long grappled with this tension. Glenn Snyder described alliances as caught between abandonment and entrapment: states seek commitments strong enough to ensure that allies will defend them, but not so expansive that they are dragged into conflicts in which their own vital interests are not at stake. Deterrence makes this balancing act harder. As Thomas Schelling argued, a commitment deters only when an adversary believes it will be honored. A military alliance therefore derives much of its value from the credibility of its promise to act together.
For the Mecca pact, therein lies the dilemma: the more unequivocal the promise, the greater the risk of entrapment; the more discretion members preserve, the greater the risk that adversaries doubt the promise altogether.
The difficulty is magnified because the three states operate in largely distinct threat environments. Pakistan’s overriding external concern remains India, its nuclear-armed rival to the east. The two countries fought major wars in 1947–48, 1965, and 1971; clashed in Kargil in 1999; and have experienced repeated military crises since, including their brief but intense confrontation in May 2025. Pakistan also faces militant violence and chronic insecurity along its western frontier. Saudi Arabia confronts Iran, the Houthis, and broader Gulf security challenges. Türkiye faces Kurdish armed groups, instability in Syria, Black Sea security concerns, NATO obligations, and an increasingly difficult relationship with Israel.
Such differences are not unusual among allies. NATO members have long disagreed over particular threats and regions. The harder problem for the Mecca pact is that its broad defense guarantee attempts to bridge three substantially different security environments. One member’s most important crisis may therefore create expectations of military support in a conflict the other two have powerful reasons to avoid.
The Houthi campaign provides the clearest indication yet of how this dilemma operates in practice. Since the Houthis declared a naval blockade of the kingdom in July, their missile and drone attacks have targeted Saudi cities, energy sites, and shipping. On September 19, Saudi air defenses intercepted a missile aimed at Riyadh. A week later, they intercepted two drones heading toward Riyadh and two ballistic missiles aimed at Khamis Mushait.
The alliance has begun responding. Türkiye’s foreign minister said on September 19 that Ankara was ready to help meet Saudi Arabia’s military needs, particularly on technical issues. On September 25, the Saudi, Pakistani, and Turkish defense chiefs and chiefs of general staff met in Riyadh under the Mecca agreement. They reviewed threats facing the kingdom and discussed intelligence cooperation, military coordination, and integration of capabilities. They also pledged to “immediately begin” translating the pact’s commitments into effective military cooperation.
But there is a meaningful difference between helping Saudi Arabia defend itself and entering another Yemen war. Pakistan and Türkiye may be willing to provide intelligence, air-defense capabilities, technical assistance, logistics, or other defensive support. Direct combat against the Houthis is another matter, and neither government has publicly announced plans to join it.
Pakistan demonstrated something similar under its bilateral defense relationship with Saudi Arabia during this year’s Iran war. Reuters reported in May that Islamabad had deployed roughly 8,000 troops, a fighter squadron, two drone squadrons, and an HQ-9 air-defense system to the kingdom, with personnel primarily serving in advisory and training roles. Pakistan, meanwhile, mediated between Washington and Tehran rather than joining offensive operations against Iran.
This is precisely where Snyder’s dilemma interacts with Schelling’s. Limited involvement reduces the danger of entrapment. Yet each limitation also communicates something about what “an attack against all” means in practice. If attacks on Saudi territory produce intelligence cooperation, air defense, and technical assistance but not direct military action against the attacker, allies and adversaries alike learn something about the boundaries of the guarantee.
Pakistan’s escalating confrontation with Afghanistan exposes the same problem from the opposite direction. Islamabad struck targets in eastern Afghanistan on September 21 and, three days later, said it had struck ten locations it described as launch and storage sites for drones used against Pakistan. Kabul rejected Pakistan’s account and said four civilians were killed.
There is no evidence that Pakistan has invoked the Mecca agreement over Afghanistan, nor that Saudi Arabia or Türkiye has been asked to participate. Pakistan is helping to operationalize collective defense in support of Saudi Arabia while confronting a serious security challenge of its own. If the confrontation with Afghanistan escalates, Riyadh and Ankara could eventually face the same question Islamabad now confronts over Saudi Arabia: how far does collective defense extend when an ally’s security crisis grows out of a complicated cross-border conflict? Supporting Pakistan’s territorial defense is one thing; becoming implicated in a Pakistan-Afghanistan conflict is another.
Türkiye presents a potentially more dangerous version of the dilemma. Its relationship with Israel has deteriorated sharply, and Syria has emerged as a possible military flashpoint. In mid-August, Israel struck Syria’s Abu al-Duhur airbase, saying Damascus was on the verge of allowing Turkish troops to deploy there. Syria’s foreign minister said no Turkish base was planned, and Türkiye’s defense ministry denied that a Turkish delegation was present at the site. Washington has said it is working to establish a deconfliction mechanism among Israel, Syria, and Türkiye, but the episode shows how competing Turkish and Israeli objectives in Syria could produce a military confrontation.
A direct Turkish-Israeli confrontation would pose difficult choices for Riyadh and Islamabad. Türkiye also belongs to NATO, so an attack on Turkish territory could, depending on the circumstances, generate consultations and political pressures under two alliance frameworks. NATO’s Article 5 obliges allies to assist an attacked member but leaves each ally discretion over the action it considers necessary, including whether to use armed force. The Mecca pact could therefore face both the problem of entangling its members in one another’s conflicts and the complications of overlapping collective-defense commitments.
Pakistan’s nuclear arsenal raises the stakes further. Nothing publicly available establishes that Islamabad has formally extended a nuclear guarantee to Saudi Arabia or Türkiye, and assuming otherwise would be a mistake. Yet deterrence operates partly through perception. Pakistan is one of nine nuclear-armed states and the pact’s only nuclear-armed member. Its arsenal was developed primarily to deter India, not to underwrite contingencies in the Gulf or the Levant. Will adversaries nevertheless perceive it as standing somewhere behind the promise that an attack on one will be treated as an attack on all?
If they do, deterrence could strengthen – but so could the consequences of entrapment. A conventional crisis involving Saudi Arabia or Türkiye could acquire a nuclear shadow none of the three governments intended.
These cases point to the same structural trade-off. A broad guarantee gives potential adversaries more reason to hesitate but expands the range of conflicts capable of implicating all three allies. A narrow guarantee protects strategic autonomy but reveals where collective action stops. The Mecca pact therefore becomes most effective as a deterrent precisely when it becomes most dangerous as an alliance.
Here the effort to avoid entrapment creates a second danger: a credibility trap. Limited involvement allows a state to avoid an unwanted war, but each limitation reveals something about how far the alliance is prepared to go. Allies may fear abandonment while adversaries learn where collective defense stops. What begins as useful strategic ambiguity can gradually become a map of the pact’s boundaries.
The three governments appear to recognize the problem. At the inaugural meeting of the pact’s Strategic Political and Defence Committee in Istanbul on August 31, their foreign and defense ministers and senior military leaders agreed to further institutionalize cooperation, establish a permanent secretariat in Saudi Arabia, strengthen defense capabilities, and ensure the “credibility and effectiveness” of collective deterrence and defense. They also stressed de-escalation and restraint. The September 25 meeting of their military chiefs suggests this process is moving from institutional design toward operational coordination

articles.full_text:
The Saudi-led coalition dismissed Sunday Houthi claims of an attack on Riyadh as “misleading” after reports of visible flames at an oil facility near the Saudi capital.
Fighting between the Iran-backed Houthis and Yemen's internationally recognized government reignited in July. The rebel group also launched numerous attacks on Saudi territory.
Government forces said Sunday they struck Houthi targets across Yemen, while the Houthis claimed the attack on the oil facility near Riyadh.
Gen. Turki al-Maliki, a spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition, told the Saudi-owned media outlet Asharq al-Awsat late Saturday the Houthis were "chasing imaginary victories."
He told the Britain-based outlet they struggled in Taiz, Yemen's third-most populous city, largely held by government forces.
Earlier Saturday, the Houthis claimed to have attacked a site south of Riyadh belonging to Saudi oil giant Aramco.
Agence France-Presse (AFP) reported flames and smoke were rising from the facility, but Saudi authorities have not commented.
Last month, the Houthis also claimed to have attacked an oil facility in the Saudi port city of Yanbu, a major oil terminal on the Red Sea.
After several years of calm, Yemen plunged back into civil war in July, pitting the Houthis, who control most of northwest Yemen including the capital Sanaa, against the country's government and its longtime Saudi backers.
The government, based in Aden, controls much of Yemen's south and east – a larger but less populated region.
Fighting has intensified. The Houthis launched a lightning offensive last month, seizing coastal regions along the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
They have also struck targets inside Saudi Arabia, the world's top oil exporter, and announced a naval blockade of its ships in the Red Sea.
Recent fighting has centered on Taiz. While the Houthis have conquered swaths of territory, they have yet to wrest control of Taiz from the government.

Yemen’s internationally recognized government has announced a major military operation against the Iran -backed Houthi rebels as they advance in the outskirts of a key city.
Meanwhile, the Iranian parliament speaker who was the lead negotiator in direct talks with the U.S. earlier this year says Washington recently put forward proposals via a mediator, without details. And a monitor says a commercial tanker has reported explosions near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait off Yemen.
Here is the latest news from the Middle East on Sunday. Full coverage is available here.
Yemen’s government declares major military operation against Houthis
Rashad al-Alimi, head of the ruling Presidential Leadership Council, made the declaration as the Iran-backed rebels advanced in the outskirts of a key southwestern city, Taiz.
Speaking from neighboring Saudi Arabia, he said the operation aims at “recovering the remaining territories” controlled by the Houthis, who made their largest land grab in recent years last month when they seized Yemen’s Red Sea coast and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
Al-Alimi called for the international community to provide support to his Saudi-backed government. In a separate statement, a Saudi military spokesperson, Maj. Gen. Turki al-Malki, stressed the kingdom’s right to take all necessary measures to deter the rebels.
The Houthis have launched a major offensive in recent days against government forces and their allies on the outskirts of Taiz, disrupting a major road linking the city to the port city of Aden, the seat of al-Alimi’s government. The rebels have besieged Taiz for more than a decade.
Earlier, the Houthis said airstrikes hit the capital, Sanaa, overnight, without giving details. The Yemeni military, backed by Riyadh, claimed responsibility, saying it struck “vital targets” in Sanaa as well as the northern province of Saada on the border with Saudi Arabia.
The escalation between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis has revived Yemen’s civil war after a four-year ceasefire.
Iran official says US has shared proposals
The United States recently put forward proposals through a mediator, Iran’s parliament speaker, Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf, told an open session of Parliament, without details.
U.S. President Donald Trump last week said he rejected Iran’s latest peace offer because it’s not good enough. Qalibaf, the lead negotiator in rare direct talks with the U.S. earlier this year, said Americans “say something different in the media.”
Qalibaf said “the era of dragging out time and dictating unilateral demands is over” and that Iran’s seven conditions for fully reopening the Strait of Hormuz remain.
Separately, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told ambassadors and chargés d’affaires of foreign missions in Tehran that “if they seek diplomatic avenues, we remain ready to reach a fair and honorable solution through diplomacy to end this war.” But he warned that any renewed military confrontation would bring a stronger response.
Araghchi also rejected a U.S. claim that the Iranian delegation had been expelled from the U.S. days after the annual U.N. gathering of world leaders, where Iran proposed a deal to the U.S. that was turned down. He said Iran had returned according to a previously arranged schedule.
Tanker reports explosions near Bab el-Mandeb Strait
A British military monitor said a commercial tanker has reported explosions “in close proximity” near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait at the southern end of the Red Sea off Yemen.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Center said the crew was reported safe and authorities were investigating after the blasts 60 nautical miles south of the port city of Mokha in Yemen. The tanker was not identified.
The Joint Maritime Information Center, overseen by the U.S. Navy, calls the threat level in the area substantial after Iran-backed Houthi rebels last month seized land next to the Strait. The rebels say they are targeting Saudi shipping.
Iran’s oil minister resigns, state media say
Iran’s oil minister resigned and President Masoud Pezeshkian accepted his resignation, state television reported. Pezeshkian appointed Hamid Bovard as caretaker oil minister following the resignation of Mohsen Paknejad. Bovard has been CEO of the National Iranian Oil Company.
The reason for the resignation was not immediately clear. It came as Iran’s oil exports face intense pressure from tightened U.S. sanctions and a naval blockade.
Iran’s ability to export oil is a crucial source of government revenue. Tehran has demanded that Washington lift sanctions on its oil sales and end the blockade as part of negotiations over reopening the Strait of Hormuz.
Israeli strikes kill 2 in Gaza, health officials say
An Israeli strike on a civilian vehicle killed one Palestinian and wounded at least 11 others, according to health officials at the Aqsa Martyrs Hospital, where the casualties were taken. Israel’s military said it targeted a known Hamas militant.
Later, a Turkish aid agency, the Deniz Feneri Association, said one of its volunteers was killed in an Israeli attack in Gaza. Israel’s military said it “eliminated” a Hamas militant whom it described as the aid group’s director.
Palestinians in Gaza have reported a surge in Israeli fire and airstrikes across the enclave over the past month. Israel says it is targeting Hamas and other militants who pose a threat, and in response to ceasefire violations, including occasional attacks.
Israeli strikes have killed at least 1,445 Palestinians in Gaza since a ceasefire was reached with the Hamas militant group nearly a year ago, according to the territory’s Health Ministry. Its figures are seen as generally reliable by U.N. agencies and independent experts. It doesn’t give a breakdown of civilians and militants. Seven Israeli soldiers have been killed in Gaza since the ceasefire.
Tanker in Strait of Hormuz struck by projectile, British military says
A projectile struck a tanker on the Strait of Hormuz, damaging the engine room, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Center said.
It was not immediately clear who launched the attack or when it was carried out. The UKMTO said the crew was reportedly safe.
In a separate report, the Joint Maritime Information Center, overseen by the U.S. Navy, said three tankers were struck on Saturday while transiting the strait, noting that attacks on the Omani side of the strait continue. That’s where the U.S. military has been guiding vessels.
Overall ship traffic on the strait has improved but remains below prewar levels, as do shipments of energy products, even though Iran has lost its near-complete grip on the crucial waterway due to the U.S. Navy’s efforts. That, along with various pipelines, has allowed Gulf countries to restore oil exports to nearly prewar levels.
Houthis claim to hit Saudi oil facilities
The Houthi military spokesperson, Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree, said the rebels fired missiles and drones at Saudi oil facilities.
In a prerecorded statement, Saree claimed to have targeted facilities of the Saudi state-run Aramco oil company, in the capital, Riyadh, and the Kurais area, which hosts a massive facility 150 kilometers (90 miles) southeast of Riyadh.
He didn’t say when it occurred, provide further details or offer evidence supporting his claim. A fire broke out at an Aramco oil refinery on Saturday, with no details released on the cause.

articles.summary: Exclusive-Saudi Arabia quietly shelving NEOM Stadium, one of 2034 World Cup venues  The Mighty 790 KFGO
articles.full_text:
By Timour Azhari and Federico Maccioni
RIYADH/DUBAI, Oct 4 (Reuters) – Saudi Arabia is quietly shelving plans to build one of its most ambitious stadiums for the 2034 FIFA World Cup, two sources familiar with the matter said, after delays and downscaling of the futuristic development housing it.
The NEOM Stadium was billed as an elevated arena in a glitzy 100-mile (160-km) steel and glass structure known as The Line, in turn part of the broader development known as NEOM.
NEOM was introduced about a decade ago as a centrepiece of de facto ruler Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s Vision 2030, an ambitious plan to diversify the economy and cut reliance on oil.
Yasir Al-Rumayyan, governor of NEOM’s owner the Public Investment Fund, confirmed in April that The Line was no longer a priority, and said it was not vital before 2030, the original delivery target for its first phase. He denied any projects had been cancelled.
However, according to two sources, plans to build the NEOM Stadium have now been shelved indefinitely.
NEOM and the Saudi government media office did not reply to requests for comment, while Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Sports redirected questions to the World Cup 2034 Hosting Higher Authority.
The Authority said “substantial delivery” of construction milestones for the event was already taking place, but did not address questions around the NEOM Stadium and costs. It shared images of some of the other stadiums under construction.
RIYADH DEVELOPING 15 VENUES FOR 2034 WORLD CUP
The 2034 World Cup is seen as a marquee event for Saudi Arabia, which under the Vision 2030 programme has invested heavily in sports via wealth fund PIF. The tournament will be the first time a single nation hosts the expanded 48-team format.
Riyadh is working to build or renovate 15 venues across five cities, as well as dozens of training facilities.
MEED Projects, a Dubai-based construction industry market intelligence platform whose team of analysts tracks tenders and projects in the region, puts the total value of the projects at $22.7 billion in data shared with Reuters.
According to MEED, NEOM’s stadium is expected to cost $2.5 billion. It lists the projected 46,000-seat stadium in its data as “on hold”.
The stadium has no listed completion date, according to the data, which describes the remaining stadiums and facilities as in various stages of development, with completion expected between 2026 and 2033.
Saudi Arabia is under increasing pressure from the Iran war, which has led to heavy disruptions to energy shipments and damage to critical infrastructure, with the kingdom facing attacks from the Iran-backed Houthis.
Last week, the Ministry of Finance said it expected a fiscal deficit this year wider than previously projected and a real GDP contraction of 3.6% following a drop in oil activities.
PIVOT FROM GIGA-PROJECTS
The geographic distribution of the stadiums adds to the challenge of delivering the projects, a third source said. That could further be compounded by some projects set to host stadiums being delayed or downsized, such as The Line or Riyadh’s New Murabba development, the source added.
In January Reuters reported that Saudi Arabia has suspended construction of The Mukaab, a colossal cube-shaped skyscraper at the centre of the New Murabba.
Reuters also reported last year that the PIF was pivoting from its focus on costly giga-projects to endeavours with more immediate financial returns, a strategy later articulated by Saudi officials.
Still, other projects for the World Cup are progressing. The Aramco Stadium in the eastern city of Al Khobar is set to be completed by the end of this year and host its first game in January, for which tickets are on sale.
Work on other planned stadiums is going ahead, a fourth source said.
(Reporting by Federico Maccioni in Dubai and Timour Azhari in Riyadh; Editing by Jan Harvey)

The stadium was set to be one of the most futuristic sports venues in Saudi Arabia’s World Cup plans, located 350 metres above ground level within the 160 km-long Neom development.
In 2024, Saudi Arabia unveiled its 2034 World Cup venue plans, with the Neom stadium among 15 proposed venues across five cities.
MEED said at the time that the stadium would seat 46,000 spectators and would be built within The Line.
Fifa chose Saudi Arabia to host the 2034 World Cup in December 2024. The tournament, which will feature 48 teams, will be the first of its kind to be played out in one country.
The latest developments cast a shadow over The Line, the new masterplan at the heart of Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s Vision 2030 economic transformation plan, which has seen the kingdom embark on an ambitious agenda of futuristic developments.
Yasir Al-Rumayyan, governor of the Public Investment Fund (PIF), which owns Neom, said in April that The Line was no longer a priority and not of utmost importance before 2030, although he stopped short of confirming that any projects had been cancelled.

Economic pressure

The PIF has reportedly been shifting away from some expensive giga-projects towards investments expected to generate financial returns more quickly.
The Neom decision comes as Saudi Arabia faces mounting economic and security pressures.
The kingdom's energy exports have been disrupted by the US-Israeli war on Iran, while Yemen's Houthi rebels have been targeting Saudi infrastructure.
On Saturday, the Houthis claimed responsibility for an attack near an Aramco facility in Riyadh. A witness reported seeing smoke and fire, although Saudi authorities and Aramco had not immediately confirmed the incident.

Yemen's internationally recognized government says it has launched a major military operation against Iran-backed Houthi rebels
Yemen's internationally recognized government has announced a major military operation against the Iran -backed Houthi rebels as they advance in the outskirts of a key city.
Meanwhile, the Iranian parliament speaker who was the lead negotiator in direct talks with the U.S. earlier this year says Washington recently put forward proposals via a mediator, without details. And Israeli strikes have killed at least two people in Gaza.
Here is the latest news from the Middle East on Sunday. Full coverage is available here.
Rashad al-Alimi, head of the ruling Presidential Leadership Council, made the declaration as the Iran-backed rebels advanced in the outskirts of a key southwestern city, Taiz.
Speaking from Saudi Arabia, he said the operation aims at “recovering the remaining territories” controlled by the Houthis, who made their largest land grab in recent years last month when they seized Yemen’s Red Sea coast and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
Al-Alimi called for the international community to provide support to his Saudi-backed government.
The Houthis have launched a major offensive in recent days against government forces and their allies on the outskirts of Taiz, disrupting a major road linking the city to the port city of Aden, the seat of al-Alimi’s government. The rebels have besieged Taiz for more than a decade.
Earlier, the Houthis said airstrikes hit the capital, Sanaa, overnight, without giving details. The Yemeni military, backed by Riyadh, claimed responsibility, saying it struck “vital targets” in Sanaa as well as the northern province of Saada on the border with Saudi Arabia.
The escalation between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis has revived Yemen’s civil war after a four-year ceasefire.
The United States recently put forward proposals through a mediator, Iran's parliament speaker, Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf, told an open session of Parliament, without details.
U.S. President Donald Trump last week said he rejected Iran’s latest peace offer because it’s not good enough. Qalibaf, the lead negotiator in rare direct talks with the U.S. earlier this year, said Americans “say something different in the media.”
Qalibaf said “the era of dragging out time and dictating unilateral demands is over” and that Iran's seven conditions for fully reopening the Strait of Hormuz remain.
Separately, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told ambassadors and chargés d’affaires of foreign missions in Tehran that “if they seek diplomatic avenues, we remain ready to reach a fair and honorable solution through diplomacy to end this war." But he warned that any renewed military confrontation would bring a stronger response.
Araghchi also rejected a U.S. claim that the Iranian delegation had been expelled from the U.S. days after the annual U.N. gathering of world leaders, where Iran proposed a deal to the U.S. that was turned down. He said Iran had returned according to a previously arranged schedule.
Iran’s oil minister resigned and President Masoud Pezeshkian accepted his resignation, state television reported. Pezeshkian appointed Hamid Bovard as caretaker oil minister following the resignation of Mohsen Paknejad.
The reason for the resignation was not immediately clear. It came as Iran’s oil exports face intense pressure from tightened U.S. sanctions and a naval blockade.
Iran’s ability to export oil is a crucial source of government revenue. Tehran has demanded that Washington lift sanctions on its oil sales and end the blockade as part of negotiations over reopening the Strait of Hormuz.
An Israeli strike on a civilian vehicle killed one Palestinian and wounded at least 11 others, according to health officials at the Aqsa Martyrs Hospital, where the casualties were taken. Israel’s military said it targeted a known Hamas militant.
Later, a Turkish aid agency, the Deniz Feneri Association, said one of its volunteers was killed in an Israeli attack in Gaza. Israel's military said it “eliminated” a Hamas militant whom it described as the aid group's director.
Palestinians in Gaza have reported a surge in Israeli fire and airstrikes across the enclave over the past month. Israel says it is targeting Hamas and other militants who pose a threat, and in response to ceasefire violations, including occasional attacks.
Israeli strikes have killed at least 1,445 Palestinians in Gaza since a ceasefire was reached with the Hamas militant group nearly a year ago, according to the territory’s Health Ministry. Its figures are seen as generally reliable by U.N. agencies and independent experts. It doesn’t give a breakdown of civilians and militants. Seven Israeli soldiers have been killed in Gaza since the ceasefire.
A projectile struck a tanker on the Strait of Hormuz, damaging the engine room, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Center said.
It was not immediately clear who launched the attack or when it was carried out. The UKMTO said the crew was reportedly safe.
The monitor in a separate report said three tankers were struck on Saturday while transiting the strait, noting that attacks on the Omani side of the strait continue. That's where the U.S. military has been guiding vessels.
Overall ship traffic on the strait has improved but remains below prewar levels, as do shipments of energy products, even though Iran has lost its near-complete grip on the crucial waterway due to the U.S. Navy’s efforts. That, along with various pipelines, has allowed Gulf countries to restore oil exports to nearly prewar levels.
The Houthi military spokesperson, Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree, said the rebels fired missiles and drones at Saudi oil facilities.
In a prerecorded statement, Saree claimed to have targeted facilities of the Saudi state-run Aramco oil company, in the capital, Riyadh, and the Kurais area, which hosts a massive facility 150 kilometers (90 miles) southeast of Riyadh.
He didn’t say when it occurred, provide further details or offer evidence supporting his claim. A fire broke out at an Aramco oil refinery on Saturday, with no details released on the cause.

articles.full_text:
A tanker was attacked in the Strait of Hormuz Sunday, a British maritime agency said, hours after Tehran warned there was no military solution to the Middle East conflict and the key waterway would remain closed until its conditions were met.
Iran has sought to impose control over the vital shipping lane since the start of its war with the United States and Israel.
It has repeatedly targeted vessels in the waterway that it accuses of transiting without its authorization, while the United States has struck ships allegedly attempting to skirt a counterblockade of Iranian ports.
An "unknown projectile" struck the ship but the crew were unharmed, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre (UKMTO) said.
No environmental impact had been recorded from the attack, it added.
The agency did not specify the date of the incident, the vessel's origin or destination, or whether it was an oil tanker or LNG carrier.
The Strait of Hormuz, through which about one fifth of the world's oil and gas transited before the war, remains a key sticking point in negotiations between Iran and the U.S.
The latest attack came just hours after Iran's parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said the Strait will not reopen until seven Iranian conditions set out in a June interim agreement are met, Iran's Nournews reported.
"The Americans, who say something different in the media, have recently put forward proposals through a mediator. But they must understand that the period of dragging out the process and dictating one-sided demands is over," Ghalibaf was quoted as saying.
"The position of the Islamic Republic of Iran is completely clear and firm, and the Strait of Hormuz will not be opened until our seven conditions, based on the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding, are met."
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said separately Sunday there was no military solution to his country's conflict with the United States, with talks on ending the war apparently at an impasse.
"If our enemies again choose the path of military confrontation, our response will be stronger than before, and we will defend ourselves with even more force," Araghchi said at a gathering of foreign ambassadors.
"There is no military solution, nor any solution based on new sanctions," he continued, adding "only negotiations based on justice and fairness" could end the conflict.
After a U.S.-Israel campaign of heavy bombardment failed to bring a decisive close to the war, Washington in recent weeks has dialed back military operations in favor of economic pressure.
The two sides agreed a memorandum of understanding in June aimed at providing a framework for a permanent resolution, but the deal collapsed, largely due to disagreements over Hormuz.
Iranian and U.S. officials last week held indirect talks on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly, with Tehran saying it presented seven conditions for reopening the strait.
Trump, however, rejected the proposal, while leaving the door open both to further talks or renewed military operations.
Araghchi reiterated that a plan put forward by Tehran to resolve its dispute with Washington could lead to the Strait of Hormuz reopening within seven days if accepted.

Nahal Toosi is POLITICO’s senior foreign affairs correspondent. She has reported on war, genocide and political chaos in a career that has taken her around the world. Her reported column delves into the decision-making of the global national security and foreign policy establishment — and the fallout that comes from it.
President Donald Trump has done a lot this year to live up to the criticism that he is reckless. But in a faceoff with a heavily armed, religiously driven regime that’s threatening a critical waterway, he’s acting remarkably restrained.
Trump may have no choice: It’s really hard to deal with the Houthis.
As the Yemeni militant group pursues a new offensive against U.S. ally Saudi Arabia, Trump has — for now — resisted entering the fray with American airstrikes. He has made clear he isn’t inclined to abandon a ceasefire the U.S. reached with the Houthis after weeks of clashes last year, despite Saudi requests for more help as the Houthis threaten oil and other commerce in the Red Sea.
Trump has stressed that the Houthis are promising not to fire on U.S. ships.
“The Houthis called us, and they don’t want to fight with us,” Trump said last month.
This is a notably cautious position from a man who has shown a big appetite for political risk this year, whether it’s by launching a war on Iran, abducting Venezuela’s president or imposing an energy blockade in an effort to oust the Cuban regime.
Standard disclaimer here: Trump frequently changes his mind, often for surprising reasons. He could end up striking the Houthis while you read this column.
Still, Trump’s unwillingness so far to break the ceasefire with the Houthis is a potential sign that he has learned some hard lessons about the battlefront, including when to avoid it.
The Houthis wouldn’t mind this being the case. In texts to me, a Houthi official sidestepped questions about the group’s views on Trump but stressed that the ceasefire with the U.S. stands.
“We do not believe there is any reason for the United States to get involved in Yemen again,” the official wrote. I granted the official, and others, anonymity to discuss sensitive issues.
Besides, Trump has other headaches. That includes deciding whether and when to resume bombing the regime in Tehran.
“The war with Iran is unresolved, so I can understand why he’s not keen to open up another front,” Tim Lenderking, a former U.S. special envoy to Yemen who has negotiated with the Houthis, told me.
There are, of course, links between the Iran war and the Saudi-Houthi fight. Iran’s regime supports and arms the Houthis, who control much of Yemen.
Tehran’s leaders and the Houthi hierarchy also share a striking number of characteristics, including leaders who stay in hiding and, some argue, expansionist ideals. Both the Houthis and Iran’s regime follow Shia Islam, though different strands. They both despise the U.S. and Israel. The Houthi official motto is: “God is the greatest, Death to America, Death to Israel, A curse upon the Jews, Victory to Islam.” Amid outside pressure, they each seek to control maritime passages key to global trade: Iran in the Strait of Hormuz and the Houthis in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
In many ways, however, the battles are distinct.
The Houthis are more a partner than a proxy for Tehran, current and former U.S. and foreign officials familiar with the group are keen to stress. The Houthis have their own grievances, history and agenda. That agenda includes ending what the Houthis describe as a blockade on Yemen imposed by Saudi Arabia, which backs the official, but weak, Yemeni government.
“We are merely defending ourselves and our country,” the Houthi official told me.
The U.S. continues to support Saudi Arabia through efforts like intelligence-sharing and weapons sales. Washington and Riyadh have a defense agreement, and, in a boilerplate statement, the White House stressed that “if it comes down to it, the United States will always stand with Saudi Arabia and support them.”
But there’s no sign that top Trump aides are urging him to again unleash the U.S. military in the Yemen fight. Last year’s U.S. air campaign against the Houthis, Operation Rough Rider, had limited impact even though Trump claimed the Houthis “capitulated.” U.S. munition shortages, caused in part by the Iran war, have to be considered now.
I’m told that Secretary of State Marco Rubio is particularly attuned to analysts’ warnings about the dangers of jumping back into the Houthi fight.
“Rubio understands the complexity. He has a good grasp of who the players are,” said a U.S. official familiar with the administration’s Middle East policy.
Some U.S. lawmakers and former U.S. officials say it’s worth helping the Saudis by carrying out airstrikes against the Houthis, at least to degrade the Yemeni militia’s capacity. Others familiar with the region warn that even sending in U.S. ground troops may not be enough to stop the group.
The Houthis have evolved into a fearsome military force in recent years. They are manufacturing more of their own weapons, while upgrading arms sent from Iran. They are even reportedly integrating artificial intelligence into their arsenal.
“They’re amazing with these advanced conventional weapons. They would take missiles and figure out how to lighten them so that they would go farther. They did trial and error with guidance systems,” said a Western official who has closely monitored the Yemen conflict. “If nothing further came from Iran, that would hurt the Houthis, but they’d overcome it.”
April Alley, a former U.N. official who has met with the Houthis, said their ambitions are likely to grow in the years ahead.
“A lot of their leadership is really young, and they’ve kind of come up in various wars. They’ve seen themselves throughout this come out of really tight spots and kind of on top, so they’re pushing on open doors,” Alley said.
Former Presidents Barack Obama and Joe Biden also struggled to counter the Houthis without tipping into large-scale conflict. So yes, Trump might have something in common with his Democratic predecessors.
Obama authorized at least one strike, casting it as a response to Houthi attacks aimed at U.S. ships, and his administration supported the Saudis in other ways. Biden authorized a series of strikes as the Houthis stepped up attacks at the height of the Gaza war while claiming to be acting against Israeli interests in the region. But Biden also scaled back U.S. military support for the Saudi war effort and pushed Riyadh to reach a 2022 truce with the Houthis.
Hussain Al-Bukhaiti, a pro-Houthi Yemeni journalist, argued that Saudi Arabia undermined that 2022 truce, especially by refusing to lift the blockade. The Houthis also allege the Saudis in July bombed an airport in Sanaa as an Iranian plane was about to land. The Houthis started striking back, and the truce collapsed.
Al-Bukhaiti blamed the Saudis for the suffering and displacement of numerous Yemeni civilians.
“It’s about Yemeni lives,” Al-Bukhaiti said. “What is silly is that we see that all the international community and the Saudis are crying out loud that the price of oil will increase and the price of shipping is increasing. I mean, what about Yemenis?”
I must interject here: The Houthis are highly repressive rulers and not great at governing. “Horrifying” is how one humanitarian official described life under the Houthis.
When I noted to Al-Bukhaiti that the Houthis struck the Saudis just as the kingdom is struggling to absorb the economic shock of the Iran war, he didn’t disagree that it was a tad opportunistic.
“It is not wrong when you take advantage of the weakness of your enemy, and our enemy is Saudi,” he said.
The Saudi Arabian Embassy in Washington declined to comment. Riyadh, which militarily intervened against the Houthis in 2015, views the militia and its ties to Iran as a next-door security risk that could eventually threaten Saudi territorial integrity.
Reuters reported Friday that the Saudis are planning a new assault on the Houthis in the coming weeks.
Trump likely wants to stay out of the Saudi-Houthi fight for as long as possible. It could get harder, though, if the Houthis grow more emboldened, threatening not just the Bab el-Mandeb Strait but also other parts of the region.
If Trump wants to avoid opening another front, it’s strange that he has devoted little diplomatic muscle to resolving the conflict.
Trump has not filled the role of the U.S. special envoy focused on the Saudi-Houthi fight; Lenderking, who last held that role, helped broker the 2022 truce. There is no one serving as U.S. ambassador to Yemen or Saudi Arabia. Trump’s favored negotiators, like Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, have their hands full with the conflicts in Iran, Gaza and Ukraine. It doesn’t help that the Omanis, who often act as mediators, don’t have the best relationship with the U.S. at the moment.
The Houthis have a diplomatic wing that deals with foreigners, often in Oman. Former international officials who have engaged with Houthi negotiators say they can be funny, charming and transactional, at least on a short-term basis.
That’s not to say diplomacy with the Houthis would be easy.
The main Houthi leadership is in Yemen, and the movement’s structure is hierarchical, religiously zealous and almost paranoid about the outside world.
Martin Griffiths, a former U.N. special envoy for Yemen, is the rare foreigner who has dealt directly with the top Houthi boss, Abdul-Malik Al-Houthi, in Yemen.
But those encounters were through screens in safe houses. (He thought he heard al-Houthi cough in a nearby room once.)

articles.title: Tanker costs soar 43-fold as Hormuz tensions reshape global oil trade - Gulf News
articles.summary: Tanker costs soar 43-fold as Hormuz tensions reshape global oil trade  Gulf News
articles.full_text:
VLCC freight rates hit record highs, reshaping Middle East oil shipping
Rates for very large crude carriers, or VLCCs, have surged to an unprecedented $1.3 million per day, according to Poten data
The figure is roughly 43 times the level recorded in early January, when the benchmark Middle East Gulf-to-Far East route cost about $30,000 per day.
At that rate, freight adds almost $33 to the cost of each barrel of crude — about 27% of its delivered cost, based on Poten’s estimate of Brent crude near $120 per barrel.
In January, freight added only about $1.73 per barrel, or roughly 3% of delivered cost.
Poten & Partners is a global leader in shipping and commodity brokerage, advisory services, and business intelligence for the energy and maritime industries.
The spike underscores how Middle East shipping disruption has transformed tanker economics. Restrictions and security risks around the Strait of Hormuz have forced longer routings, more ship-to-ship transfers and higher war-risk premiums, while tying up a growing share of the global VLCC fleet in the Gulf of Oman.
Clarksons Research earlier reported average global VLCC spot earnings approaching $642,000 per day, while some Middle East-to-Asia routes had already exceeded $1 million per day.
Saudi export flows and shuttle operations through Hormuz have further tightened vessel availability.
For refiners and traders, the result is a sharp rise in landed crude costs even before insurance, financing and port charges. The freight surge may also influence sourcing decisions, with buyers weighing alternative supply regions against the cost of moving oil through the disrupted Gulf corridor.
A VLCC is a supertanker capable of carrying about 2 million barrels of crude, making it central to long-haul oil trade from the Gulf to Asia.
Its day rate is therefore highly sensitive to disruptions at the Strait of Hormuz, the chokepoint linking Gulf producers with global markets.
The $1.3 million figure should be read as a reported market assessment rather than a universal rate: VLCC pricing varies sharply by route, vessel availability, cargo size, insurance and war-risk exposure.
Still, multiple freight assessments show the same direction — a historic spike driven by Hormuz-related disruption and scarce tanker capacity.

According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Ship Tanks market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture.
The global ship tanks market is entering a transformative decade as it balances rising demand for liquid bulk transport with the imperative to decarbonize maritime operations. Ship tanks, the specialized containment systems aboard tankers, gas carriers, and tank barges, form the backbone of international trade in crude oil, refined products, chemicals, and liquefied gases. As of 2026, the market is shaped by a dual dynamic: robust energy trade flows sustaining demand for conventional tankers, and accelerating investment in LNG and LPG carrier capacity as nations diversify energy sources.
Shipyards in East Asia, particularly China, South Korea, and Japan, dominate newbuild activity, while retrofitting and maintenance demand grows across established fleets. Regulatory pressures from the International Maritime Organization are pushing adoption of advanced coatings, alternative fuels, and digital monitoring systems, raising the technical bar for tank fabrication. The forecast horizon to 2035 points to moderate but steady growth, with a CAGR of 3.2%, as fleet renewal cycles, emerging trade routes, and the energy transition reshape demand patterns.
This report provides a data-driven view of market size, segmentation, supply chain dynamics, and competitive forces, equipping stakeholders with actionable insights for strategic planning.
The baseline scenario for the global ship tanks market through 2035 anticipates steady expansion, supported by sustained demand for liquid bulk transportation and the gradual replacement of aging tonnage. Global seaborne trade in crude oil and refined products remains a foundational driver, though its growth rate is expected to moderate as energy efficiency improves and some demand shifts toward alternative sources. The more dynamic growth vector is liquefied natural gas (LNG), where expanding export capacity in the United States, Qatar, and Australia is fueling orders for new LNG carriers, each requiring sophisticated membrane or Moss-type containment systems.
Chemical tanker demand is also projected to rise, driven by growth in specialty chemicals and stricter safety standards that favor modern, coated tank designs. On the supply side, shipyards in China and South Korea are investing in automation and digitalization to improve productivity and meet tighter delivery schedules. However, the market faces headwinds from volatile steel prices, skilled labor shortages, and regulatory uncertainty surrounding future fuel choices. The baseline forecast assumes no major global recession and a gradual, orderly energy transition. Under these conditions, the market index is expected to reach 137 by 2035 (2025=100), reflecting a 3.2% CAGR.
This outlook underscores the importance of technological differentiation and supply chain resilience for market participants.
Crude oil transport remains the largest end-use segment for ship tanks, underpinned by global energy demand and long-haul seaborne trade. Despite the energy transition, crude oil is expected to remain a dominant fuel source through 2035, particularly in emerging economies. Demand for very large crude carriers (VLCCs) and Suezmax tankers will be sustained by oil flows from the Middle East, West Africa, and the Americas to refineries in Asia. However, growth will be tempered by efficiency gains, pipeline expansions, and gradual substitution by renewables. The segment's demand is closely tied to global GDP growth, oil price differentials, and refinery utilization rates.
Through 2035, fleet renewal will be a key driver as older, less efficient tonnage is scrapped and replaced with dual-fuel or scrubber-fitted vessels. Tank fabrication will increasingly focus on corrosion-resistant materials and enhanced safety features to meet stricter environmental and safety standards. Current trend: Stable with moderate growth.
Major trends: Shift toward dual-fuel and methanol-ready tankers to comply with emissions regulations, Growing share of Asian refiners in global crude imports, favoring larger vessel sizes, Increased scrapping of older single-hull and early double-hull tankers, and Adoption of digital monitoring for cargo integrity and predictive maintenance.

Refined petroleum transport, encompassing gasoline, diesel, jet fuel, and other products, is a critical segment for ship tanks. Demand is driven by regional imbalances between refining capacity and consumption, with major export hubs in the U.S. Gulf Coast, India, and the Middle East supplying import-dependent markets in Europe, Africa, and Latin America. The segment is experiencing a shift toward larger, more efficient product tankers as trade routes lengthen and cargoes become more diverse. Stricter sulfur regulations are prompting investment in scrubbers and low-sulfur fuel compatibility, influencing tank design and materials. Through 2035, growth will be supported by rising petrochemical demand and the need to replace aging tonnage.
However, the pace of growth will be moderated by the increasing adoption of electric vehicles and biofuels in developed markets, which could reduce gasoline and diesel demand. Tank fabrication will emphasize flexibility to handle multiple product grades and minimize contamination risks. Current trend: Growing with product trade shifts.

Chemical transport is a high-value segment requiring specialized ship tanks with advanced corrosion-resistant coatings and precise temperature control. Demand is driven by the global expansion of the chemical industry, particularly in Asia-Pacific, where rapid industrialization and urbanization are boosting consumption of specialty chemicals, polymers, and intermediates. Chemical tankers are typically smaller and more complex than oil tankers, with multiple segregated tanks and sophisticated pumping systems. The segment is expected to grow faster than crude and product transport, supported by rising trade in hazardous and high-purity chemicals.
Through 2035, stricter environmental and safety regulations will drive demand for double-hulled, coated, and stainless-steel tanks. The shift toward green chemistry and bio-based chemicals may also create new requirements for tank materials and cleaning protocols. Fleet renewal and retrofitting will be key, as older chemical tankers are replaced with more efficient and compliant vessels. Current trend: Accelerating due to specialty chemicals.

LNG trade is projected to grow significantly through 2035, with major export projects in the United States, Qatar, and Australia coming online. This will require a substantial increase in LNG carrier capacity, each equipped with sophisticated membrane or Moss-type containment systems. LPG carriers are also in demand, supported by rising petrochemical feedstock needs and residential heating in emerging markets.
The segment demands highly engineered tanks capable of withstanding cryogenic temperatures and strict safety standards. articles.full_text:
A major investment forum, organised by the Ministry of foreign affairs jointly with the Ministry of finance and economy, concluded in the capital of Turkmenistan. This large-scale event became a prestigious platform for dialogue, bringing together high-ranking representatives of government agencies, international financial institutions, industry organisations, and leading foreign companies.
Forum participants focused on developing regional infrastructure and deepening both bilateral and multilateral cooperation. One of the significant events of the business program was the speech by Mahdi Heidari, deputy minister of economy and finance of the Islamic Republic of Iran, who emphasised the strategic importance of the partnership with Turkmenistan.
In his speech, the representative of the Iranian delegation noted that participation in the Ashgabat forum is a valuable opportunity to reaffirm historical, friendly, and strategic ties with Turkmenistan, as well as to demonstrate determination to expand economic cooperation.
According to M. Heidari, modern investments in the region go beyond local national markets. The main objective is to create a single economic space linking the markets of Iran, Turkmenistan and all of Central Asia.
«The foundation for such integration is the International «North-South» Transport Corridor, the Middle Corridor, and the active development of logistics links between the Caspian region, the Persian Gulf, and global trade routes. In this context, Iran is ready to provide public and private entities from Turkmenistan and Central Asian countries with direct access to Persian Gulf ports and Middle Eastern markets. In turn, Turkmenistan serves as a strategic bridge for Iran to the broader Eurasian economic space. We must view investment not simply as a movement of capital from one country to another, but as a tool for building strong regional economic connectivity», – the Iranian economist emphasised.
During the presentation, four key areas were outlined in detail that could become drivers of a new stage of economic cooperation.
The first – energy. There are ample opportunities here to exploit the potential of gas swap supplies, develop infrastructure for the transportation, storage and processing of energy resources, and deepen cooperation in the petrochemical industry.
The second – transit and logistics. Targeted investment in the modernisation of railways and roads, bridges, border terminals, and logistics centers in the Caspian sea will significantly reduce the time and cost of regional trade.
The third – agriculture and food industry. Combining the agricultural production of Central Asian countries with Iranian processing, packaging, and rapid delivery capabilities will enable joint access to international markets.
And the fourth sphere is industrial investments. Here, it is necessary to actively utilize the potential of free and special economic zones, which provide investors with a unified platform with access to domestic and transit routes.
The deputy minister of economy and finance of Iran reminded that Tehran and Ashgabat have a wealth of historical experience in successfully implementing large-scale joint projects.
In this regard, the main call of the speaker was the need to transform existing experience into a «new generation of investments» that is, projects that will create sustainable supply chains, strengthen national economies, and serve the well-being of peoples. The Iranian side expressed its readiness for open and constructive dialogue with both its Turkmen colleagues and all interested international investors.

articles.title: Unprecedented US Military Buildup in the Middle East and Iranian Alertness in the Strait of Hormuz - alquds.com
articles.summary: Unprecedented US Military Buildup in the Middle East and Iranian Alertness in the Strait of Hormuz  alquds.com
articles.full_text:
The Middle East region is experiencing extensive US military movements, as informed sources announced the deployment of a third aircraft carrier to the region to reinforce existing forces. This military buildup is the largest of its kind since the 2003 invasion of Iraq, indicating the seriousness of current tensions in the region.
The aircraft carrier 'Theodore Roosevelt' is heading from its base in San Diego, California, to join the aircraft carriers 'George Washington' and 'George H.W. Bush'. This move aims to enhance the deterrent capabilities of the United States in light of escalating mutual threats with Tehran.
According to press reports, the Pentagon plans to increase the number of US troops in the region to three full combat groups by next November. These groups are expected to include approximately 20,000 soldiers and up to 150 advanced fighter jets.
In addition to the aircraft carriers, Washington has sent guided-missile destroyers and the amphibious 'Makin Island' group, which includes three specialized ships. These vessels are accompanied by thousands of Marine Corps personnel to enhance combat readiness in various conditions.
Estimates indicate that the total number of US forces in the region could exceed 50,000 personnel after the arrival of the latest reinforcements. This figure includes approximately 7,000 sailors and an additional 2,000 elite Marine Corps troops.
In parallel with naval movements, Washington has significantly strengthened its air defense systems in the Arabian Gulf region. Two additional 'Patriot' missile batteries have been sent to protect vital oil and gas installations from any potential attacks.
In response, Tehran has escalated its threats regarding navigation in the strategic Strait of Hormuz, asserting its full control over the waterway. Revolutionary Guard commanders stated that Iranian forces are monitoring all movements and will not allow any hostile approach to their borders.
Iranian sources revealed a new bill in parliament aimed at regulating the national administration of the Strait of Hormuz to serve security interests. The bill stipulates a ban on the passage of ships belonging to the Israeli occupation or any countries classified by Tehran as hostile.
The proposed law also requires ships from non-hostile countries to obtain prior permits from the General Staff of the Iranian Armed Forces. This measure aims to impose strict control over arms and military equipment shipments passing through the strait.
Former Iranian diplomats believe that the current US buildup will not achieve its political or military objectives in pressuring Tehran. They affirmed that Iran has faced more severe economic and military pressures in the past and has not backed down from its national principles.
Political readings in Tehran suggest that this military escalation may be a prelude to broader operations after the US midterm elections. However, Iranian sources emphasize that their first option remains the diplomatic and peaceful path to avoid the outbreak of a full-scale war.
For his part, a former US Assistant Secretary of Defense considered that the purpose of sending the third aircraft carrier still holds multiple possibilities. The action could be routine to replace exhausted forces, or an actual reinforcement to carry out potential military strikes based on presidential orders.
The former official explained that the final picture of US movements will become clear once the naval units reach their final deployment locations. If the three carriers remain together, it means a real readiness for a direct military confrontation with Iranian forces.
Regional and international capitals are awaiting the outcomes of this unprecedented military buildup and its impact on the stability of global energy markets. In the absence of direct communication channels, the risk of field miscalculation remains between the two powers in the Gulf waters.
This military buildup, whether for pressure or escalation, will not succeed in deterring Iran from its firm positions or achieving Washington's goals.
