articles.title: Ethiopian rebel forces withdraw from Tigray regional capital - BBC
articles.summary: Ethiopian rebel forces withdraw from Tigray regional capital  BBCFighting in Ethiopia raises fears of wider war, from Horn of Africa to Red Sea  The Washington PostGovernment forces seize capital of Ethiopia's Tigray region from rebels  ReutersEthiopia’s forces retake Mekelle amid renewed Tigray fighting  Al JazeeraEthiopian federal forces control Tigray capital as regional rivals meet in Egypt  France 24
articles.full_text:
Rebel forces in Ethiopia's northern Tigray region have said they have temporarily withdrawn from the regional capital, Mekelle, as fighting with the national army moves towards the city.
The Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), which has been running the region, said its decision to relocate was made because of concerns about risks to civilians.
Two residents in Mekelle told the BBC that pro-government forces now control the city and TPLF forces have abandoned it. One resident also said mobile phone services appear to have resumed in parts of the city.
Fighting has erupted in recent weeks between the TPLF and federal government forces alongside allied fighters in parts of Ethiopia's northern regions of Tigray, Afar and Amhara.
The development marks a major shift in the conflict and raises concerns among observers that the fighting could further destabilise the Horn of Africa, potentially drawing in neighbouring countries.
The US Department of State called for "restraint" and "dialogue" on all sides ahead of a diplomatic meeting about the conflict in Egypt on Sunday with leaders from some of Ethiopia's neighbours.
Tigray residents have been trying to recover from a devastating two-year civil war that ended in 2022 when the African Union (AU) brokered a peace deal, known as the Pretoria Agreement, between the two sides.
However, in the last six months there has been a worsening of relations, with both sides accusing each other of violating the agreement.
Last month, the TPLF joined six other armed movements, including the Fano militia from Amhara, to form an alliance whose stated objective is to remove Ethiopia's Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government from power.
The civil war was one of the most deadly conflicts this century - the AU's mediator estimated some 600,000 people died as the fighting drove the region to the precipice of famine.
On Friday, neighbours Ethiopia and Eritrea severed diplomatic relations with each other after Addis Ababa accused Asmara of supporting a new rebel alliance - an allegation that it denied.
Ethiopia has also accused Egypt of supporting the rebels, leading to the expulsion of an Egyptian diplomat, which Cairo responded to by ordering an Ethiopian embassy official to leave within the same period.
The United Nations has warned that the deteriorating security situation in northern Ethiopia is severely disrupting humanitarian work and has called on all sides to guarantee safe and unhindered access to people in need.

articles.title: Turkish officials visit Riyadh as Mecca alliance gains momentum
articles.summary: Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan will be joined by National Defense Minister Yaşar Güler and Chief of General Staff Selçuk Bayraktaroğlu on a visit to Saudi Arabia’s Riyadh on Monday....
articles.full_text:
Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan will be joined by National Defense Minister Yaşar Güler and Chief of General Staff Selçuk Bayraktaroğlu on a visit to Saudi Arabia’s Riyadh on Monday.
They will attend a meeting of the Strategic Political and Defense Committee of the historic Mecca Joint Defense Alliance, formed by Türkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan in August. The meeting comes amid rising threats to Saudi Arabia by the Houthis in Yemen.
Foreign Ministry sources said on Sunday that Fidan would reaffirm Türkiye’s strong solidarity with and support for Saudi Arabia in the face of Houthi attacks and underline that provocative acts targeting sacred sites are unacceptable. Saudi Arabia is the birthplace of Islam and home to its most sacred site, the Kaaba, located in Mecca. Mecca has recently come under fire from the Houthis.
The Houthi group said on Saturday that it targeted Saudi oil company Aramco in Riyadh with ballistic missiles and drones in response to attacks on the Yemeni capital, Sanaa.
The operation “successfully achieved its objective,” causing fires at the targeted sites, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said in a televised statement.
Saree added that Sanaa and other provinces had been subjected to 60 airstrikes over the last 24 hours, bringing the total number of strikes to 1,420. He attributed the attacks to Saudi Arabia.
The spokesperson warned that the group would respond to “blockade with blockade, and escalation with escalation.”
Meanwhile, Turki al-Maliki, spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen’s government, said in remarks carried by Saudi media, including Asharq Al-Awsat, that Houthi claims of targeting Riyadh on Saturday were “misleading.”
He added that the Houthis were trying to “divert attention from the scale of their losses and growing public anger over the militias’ conduct and their ties to foreign agendas that have brought chaos and destruction to Yemen.”
Since March 2015, Saudi Arabia has led a military coalition supporting Yemen’s internationally recognized government against Houthi forces, which have controlled Sanaa and several other governorates since September 2014.
In July this year, the Houthis announced a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia, saying the move was in response to a Saudi naval and air siege on areas under their control in Yemen. The group has since targeted energy infrastructure in the kingdom.
President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, Pakistani Prime Minister Muhammad Shahbaz Sharif and Saudi Crown Prince and Prime Minister Mohammed bin Salman Al Saud signed the Mecca agreement for joint defense in Mecca on Aug. 7, 2026. The agreement aims to bolster the security of Türkiye, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia through joint deterrence and defense, and reflects the three countries’ commitment to developing regional solutions to regional issues and their shared strategic vision centered on regional security and stability.
A Strategic Political and Defense Committee, comprising the foreign and defense ministers and chiefs of general staff of the three countries, was established to guide activities under the agreement. The committee held its inaugural meeting in Istanbul on Aug. 31, 2026. At the meeting, foundational decisions were adopted, and technical work toward institutionalizing the alliance was reviewed. Accordingly, the alliance’s secretariat is expected to be established in Riyadh as soon as possible. Retired Pakistani Lt. Gen. Nauman Mahmood has been nominated to serve as its first secretary-general.
The foreign ministers of the three countries held a meeting in New York on Sept. 24, 2026, on the sidelines of the High-Level Week of the 81st United Nations General Assembly. Regional developments were discussed at the meeting. In a joint statement issued afterward, the three countries condemned attacks targeting the holy city of Mecca and Saudi Arabia’s civilian and economic infrastructure. The chiefs of general staff of the three countries met in Riyadh on Sept. 25, 2026.
Turkish sources said Fidan would convey Türkiye’s views on the next steps for the alliance and its institutionalization process. He will also offer Türkiye’s assessment of threats to peace and stability in the Middle East and views on regional developments related to the joint security of the allies. He is also expected to highlight how the alliance’s progress in a short time has proved valuable for the prospects of lasting stability in the region, as well as the importance of the alliance both in building capacity for a joint and efficient response to existing threats and in preventing regional crises.
Fidan is also expected to underline the prioritization of peaceful means to resolve conflicts in the region and the need to avoid steps that may escalate tensions. He will also stress the importance of ensuring the freedom and security of navigation on international trade routes and discuss how Israel has continued to undermine efforts for regional peace and stability.
In an interview last month, Fidan said the alliance had reached an advanced stage, with efforts underway to establish its headquarters and assign personnel, describing the initiative as a “very game-changing platform.” Fidan also implied that Türkiye stood ready to provide technical assistance to Saudi Arabia amid an escalating conflict with the Houthis in Yemen.
Fidan stated that there is “a very strong will” behind the alliance and that Ankara is working to turn that political will into action.
“The Mecca alliance is really at a good stage. There’s a very strong will that has been put forward. We’re working with all our strength to put this will into action,” Fidan told broadcaster NTV last month.
He said steps toward institutionalizing the alliance are underway, particularly work to establish a secretariat envisaged under the agreement and a military headquarters affiliated with it. He added that detailed preparations for both structures have “almost been completed” and that the three countries have reached a common understanding of how they will operate.
“There are steps currently being taken toward institutionalization. In particular, the work on establishing the secretariat mentioned in the agreement and bringing an affiliated military headquarters into operation is almost complete. We have reached a common understanding. From now on, the remaining stage is to send personnel and make the headquarters operational. I am pleased with the process on this issue,” Fidan said.
He said that once institutionalization steps are completed, talks could be held with the other two founding countries on admitting new members.
“There is such a principle decision because our president said this from the beginning. If this does not grow, then it would not be an alliance area. We would have created a bloc. Our regional vision is for as many countries in the region as possible to come together and establish a common defense area.
“This defense area is not against outsiders; it is about solving problems within the region better through regional ownership and creating an environment of trust that has not existed before, in order to prevent new crises from emerging. The basic point of departure for all of this is the search for regional solutions to regional problems,” Fidan said.
He stressed that the alliance was not intended to create a new regional bloc against other countries but to establish a common defense framework based on regional ownership.
“It is an alliance open to the countries of the region,” he said.

articles.title: Oil and Gas Market Outlook to 2035 - IndexBox
articles.summary: Oil and Gas Market Outlook to 2035  IndexBox
articles.full_text:
Abstract
According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Oil And Gas market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture.
The global oil and gas market enters 2026 at a pivotal inflection point, balancing resilient hydrocarbon demand against accelerating energy transition pressures. This report provides a comprehensive analysis of the market's current state, dissecting supply, demand, trade, and price dynamics that define the industry. The analysis projects trends and strategic implications through 2035, a period expected to see increasing market volatility and a redefinition of competitive success. While renewable energy sources gain traction, hydrocarbons are projected to remain a cornerstone of the global energy mix, underpinning industrial activity, transportation, and petrochemical manufacturing.
However, the growth trajectory is uneven, with regional demand patterns diverging sharply based on economic development, policy mandates, and technological adoption. The industry's future will be shaped by its ability to navigate decarbonization mandates, geopolitical fragmentation, and evolving investment criteria. This report serves as an essential strategic tool for industry participants, investors, policymakers, and stakeholders seeking to understand the multifaceted forces at play.
By providing a data-driven, objective foundation, it enables informed decision-making regarding capital allocation, risk management, market entry, and long-term strategic positioning in an increasingly complex and transitional global energy landscape.
The baseline scenario for the world oil and gas market from 2026 to 2035 anticipates moderate growth, with global consumption expanding at a compound annual growth rate of 1.2% and the market index reaching 112.7 by 2035 (2025=100). This outlook assumes a gradual pace of energy transition, sustained economic growth in developing economies, and continued investment in upstream and midstream infrastructure. Demand for natural gas, particularly LNG, is expected to grow faster than oil, driven by power generation and industrial applications in Asia.
Refined petroleum product demand will plateau in developed regions but rise in emerging markets, supported by transportation and petrochemical feedstock needs. Supply-side dynamics will be shaped by OPEC+ production policies, US shale output, and new LNG liquefaction projects. Price volatility is likely to persist due to geopolitical tensions and inventory fluctuations. The baseline scenario does not assume radical policy shifts or technological breakthroughs that would drastically alter the energy mix before 2035. Key risks include faster-than-expected EV adoption, carbon pricing, and supply disruptions.
Overall, the market remains vital to the global economy, but growth will be increasingly concentrated in specific segments and regions.
Demand Drivers and Constraints
Primary Demand Drivers
- Rising industrial feedstock demand in emerging economies, particularly for petrochemical production
- Expanding LNG trade and infrastructure, enabling gas market globalization
- Transportation fuel demand growth in developing countries amid rising vehicle fleets
- Power generation fuel switching from coal to natural gas in key markets
- Residential and commercial heating needs in colder regions
- Marine bunkering and aviation fuel demand tied to global trade and travel
Potential Growth Constraints
- Accelerating adoption of electric vehicles and renewable energy reducing oil demand
- Stringent decarbonization policies and carbon pricing in developed economies
- Geopolitical tensions and supply disruptions causing price volatility
- Underinvestment in upstream projects due to energy transition uncertainty
- Efficiency improvements and substitution effects lowering intensity of use
Demand Structure by End-Use Industry
End-Use Industry Demand Split (%)
Transportation Fuel (estimated share: 45%)
Transportation fuel remains the largest end-use sector for oil and gas, encompassing gasoline, diesel, and jet fuel. In 2026, demand is supported by global road freight, passenger vehicles, and aviation activity. Through 2035, growth will be uneven: OECD countries will see declining gasoline demand due to EV adoption and efficiency standards, while non-OECD economies, especially in Asia and Africa, will experience rising fuel consumption as vehicle ownership expands. Diesel demand will be sustained by industrial and commercial transport, while jet fuel recovers to pre-pandemic levels and grows with air travel. Key demand-side indicators include vehicle sales, miles traveled, and freight tonnage.
The sector's share will gradually erode but remain dominant, with alternative fuels making inroads slowly. Major companies include Exxon Mobil, Shell, BP, and Chevron. Current trend: Moderate growth in developing markets, plateau in developed economies.
Major trends: Electrification of light-duty vehicles in developed markets, Rising demand for diesel in emerging economies, Aviation fuel demand recovery and growth, Biofuels blending mandates increasing, and Efficiency improvements in internal combustion engines.
Representative participants: Exxon Mobil, Shell, BP, Chevron, and TotalEnergies.
Power Generation (estimated share: 20%)
Power generation is a key end-use for natural gas, and increasingly for oil in some regions. In 2026, gas-fired power plants provide reliable and flexible electricity, complementing renewables. Through 2035, demand for natural gas in power generation will grow as countries seek to reduce coal dependence and meet emissions targets. LNG imports will enable gas use in regions lacking pipeline infrastructure. Demand-side indicators include electricity consumption, capacity additions, and fuel-switching policies. However, competition from renewables and battery storage will temper growth in some markets. Major companies involved include Gazprom, Equinor, and PetroChina. Current trend: Strong growth for natural gas, coal-to-gas switching.
Major trends: Coal-to-gas switching in Asia, Growth of LNG-fired power plants, Integration with renewable energy grids, Carbon capture and storage adoption, and Policy support for cleaner fossil fuels.
Representative participants: Gazprom, Equinor, PetroChina, Shell, and TotalEnergies.
Industrial Feedstock (estimated share: 15%)
Industrial feedstock, primarily naphtha and natural gas liquids, is essential for petrochemical production. In 2026, demand is strong for plastics, fertilizers, and chemicals. Through 2035, this sector will see the fastest growth among oil and gas end-uses, driven by rising global consumption of consumer goods and packaging. Demand-side indicators include petrochemical capacity additions, plastics production, and industrial output. The shift to lighter feedstocks in the US and Middle East will influence trade flows. Major companies include Saudi Aramco, Exxon Mobil, and Dow Chemical. Current trend: Robust growth driven by petrochemical demand.
Major trends: Expansion of petrochemical capacity in Asia and Middle East, Shift to ethane and LPG feedstocks, Growth in demand for plastics and synthetic fibers, Circular economy initiatives impacting feedstock demand, and Integration of refineries with petrochemical complexes.
Representative participants: Saudi Aramco, Exxon Mobil, Dow Chemical, Sinopec, and LyondellBasell.
Heating and Residential Use (estimated share: 10%)
Heating and residential use encompasses natural gas, heating oil, and LPG for space heating, cooking, and hot water. In 2026, demand is concentrated in colder regions like North America, Europe, and parts of Asia. Through 2035, growth will be limited by energy efficiency improvements and a shift to electric heat pumps in developed markets. However, in developing countries, rising incomes and urbanization will boost demand for LPG and natural gas. Demand-side indicators include household formation, heating degree days, and appliance penetration. Major companies include Shell, BP, and local distribution companies. Current trend: Stable in cold regions, declining in mild climates.
Major trends: Electrification of heating in Europe and North America, Growth of LPG use in developing countries, Energy efficiency retrofits reducing demand, Policy incentives for heat pumps, and Weather variability impacting seasonal demand.
Representative participants: Shell, BP, TotalEnergies, Eni, and Local utilities.
Marine Bunkering and Aviation Fuel (estimated share: 10%)
Marine bunkering and aviation fuel represent specialized demand segments. In 2026, marine bunkering is dominated by heavy fuel oil, but IMO 2020 regulations have increased use of low-sulfur fuels and LNG. Aviation fuel demand is recovering and growing with air travel. Through 2035, marine bunkering will see a gradual shift to LNG, methanol, and biofuels, while aviation fuel demand will grow steadily, especially in Asia-Pacific. Demand-side indicators include global trade volumes, air passenger kilometers, and fleet composition. Major companies include BP, Shell, and Chevron. Current trend: Moderate growth, with marine shifting to cleaner fuels.
Major trends: IMO regulations driving low-sulfur fuel adoption, LNG as marine fuel gaining traction, Aviation fuel demand growth in emerging markets, Sustainable aviation fuel mandates, and Slowdown in global trade affecting bunkering.
Representative participants: BP, Shell, Chevron, Exxon Mobil, and TotalEnergies.

articles.title: Alex Matrsson: Qatar Contributes to a Stronger Regional Industrial Identity at Made in GCC 2026 - dknews.kz

articles.full_text:
In an exclusive Senior Advisor interview, Mr. Alex Matrsson, the Swedish Pracademic and International Business Strategist, regards Qatar’s participation in Made in GCC 2026, taking place from 6 to 8 October 2026 at Exhibition World Bahrain, as a notable demonstration of the country’s industrial confidence and regional economic engagement. Announced by the Ministry of Commerce and Industry on September 2026, the Qatari participation includes the Qatar pavilion, Qatar Development Bank, Qatar Economic Zones Company and more than 20 Qatari factories. For Mr. Matrsson, the composition of the delegation is significant because it places manufacturing, investment and institutional support together on one GCC platform.
Turning Qatar National Vision 2030 into Industrial Presence
Mr. Matrsson sees a direct connection between this participation and Qatar National Vision 2030. The Qatari pavilion provides an opportunity to present national manufacturing capabilities, specialised industrial clusters, investment opportunities and value-added products to a regional audience. In his assessment, this gives economic diversification a practical dimension: national development is being represented through companies, production capabilities and institutions capable of engaging with markets beyond Qatar.
The participation of Qatar Development Bank and Qatar Economic Zones Company adds another layer. Rather than presenting factories in isolation, Qatar is bringing elements of the wider industrial ecosystem that supports business development and investment. Mr. Matrsson considers this particularly relevant for international business because investors and commercial partners generally look beyond individual products to the institutional environment surrounding production and expansion.
The Ministry’s latest figures provide context for Qatar’s presence. Industrial-sector investment stood at QAR 248.44 billion in the second quarter of 2026. Eleven factories began production during the quarter, while 28 factories had commenced production during the first half of the year with combined investments of QAR 253 million. Exporting factories represented 25 percent of the total in the second quarter, compared with 23 percent in the first quarter, while private-sector exports rose by 12.5 percent. Mr. Matrsson sees these developments as evidence of an industrial sector increasingly oriented toward production, export activity and market expansion.
A Broad Manufacturing Base
The range of industries represented by Qatar is also important. Aluminium, plastics, cables, glass, pharmaceuticals, food products and engineering are among the sectors identified in connection with the participation. Mr. Matrsson regards this diversity as a strategic asset because it gives Qatar multiple avenues for cooperation with companies and industries across the GCC.
Made in GCC 2026 provides an appropriate setting for that engagement. The event combines an exhibition of GCC-made products and industrial solutions with a forum involving government representatives, business leaders, investors and experts. Its focus on industrial integration, supply chains, technology, smart manufacturing, financing and international competitiveness gives Qatar an opportunity to position its industrial capabilities within the wider economic transformation taking place across the Gulf.
Qatar and Bahrain: Complementary National Visions
Mr. Matrsson also places Qatar’s participation within the constructive role played by Bahrain as host of the inaugural event. Held under the patronage of His Majesty King Hamad bin Isa Al Khalifa, King of the Kingdom of Bahrain, the forum demonstrates Bahrain’s commitment to creating platforms for regional economic cooperation. Bahrain Economic Vision 2030 and Qatar National Vision 2030 have different national priorities, yet both provide frameworks for diversification, competitiveness, investment and sustainable economic development.
The participation also reflects the strategic direction under the leadership of His Highness Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani, Amir of the State of Qatar. Mr. Matrsson regards His Highness’s leadership as an important force behind Qatar’s continued commitment to economic diversification, national industrial development and international engagement. In this context, Qatar’s presence at Made in GCC 2026 can be viewed as a practical expression of the country’s long-term vision, combining institutional capability, private-sector participation and an outward-looking approach to regional economic cooperation.
The same principle can be seen across the GCC, where national visions provide distinct development pathways while creating areas of common interest. Mr. Matrsson considers this convergence particularly valuable in manufacturing, technology, logistics, investment and trade. Strong national economies can provide the foundation for stronger regional economic relationships, provided cooperation respects the individual capabilities and priorities of each member state.
For Qatar, the immediate opportunity is commercial as much as institutional. The Ministry identifies the potential to connect Qatari producers with buyers, distributors and strategic partners while opening access to new markets. Mr. Matrsson considers these connections more consequential than exhibition visibility alone. The real measure of participation will be whether conversations develop into partnerships, distribution relationships, investment and sustained trade.
Qatar’s Contribution to a Stronger GCC Industrial Identity
The wider ambition of Made in GCC is to strengthen recognition of Gulf-made products and establish a more unified identity around their quality and competitiveness. Mr. Matrsson sees Qatar’s substantial presence as an important contribution to that objective. Qatari manufacturers are not simply appearing within a regional showcase; they are participating in a platform through which the industrial capabilities of GCC states can become more visible and commercially connected.
In conclusion, Mr. Alex Matrsson, the Swedish Pracademic and International Business Strategist, highlights that Qatar’s participation in Made in GCC 2026 demonstrates how national industrial development can reinforce regional economic cooperation. Qatar brings established institutions, expanding manufacturing activity and a diverse group of national producers to Bahrain, while the event creates a setting for practical engagement with the wider GCC market. For Mr. Matrsson, the significance rests in this connection between Qatar National Vision 2030, the Kingdom of Bahrain’s Economic Vision 2030 and the broader strategic direction of GCC leadership, with industrial cooperation providing a practical pathway from national ambition to regional economic value.

Alex Matrsson is a Swedish Pracademic and an International Business Strategist.
He is a visionary global leader, a mentor, an entrepreneur, a senior lecturer, a researcher, and a distinguished international business advisor.
He is the number one International Business Strategy graduate in Sweden.
He has extensive experience initiating, running, and managing businesses across the global value chain, as well as working internationally with investors, SMEs, MNCs, government agencies, universities, and multidisciplinary research institutes.
Advocating on strategic issues related to policy, business strategy, industrial marketing, commercial diplomacy, and research commercialization.

Therefore, these concepts jointly constitute the springboard for his knowledge dissemination endeavors.

He aims to enable the students to operationalize their "state-of-the-art" knowledge constructively—so that they can become an invaluable source of prosperity, driving forward the "social" and "economic" well-being for their local communities, their regions, and the larger society, worldwide.
His scientific endeavors consolidate around trade promotion, emerging markets, business resilience, and the network approach to internationalization.

articles.title: Iran says Strait of Hormuz will not reopen until conditions are met - GMA News Online
articles.summary: Iran says Strait of Hormuz will not reopen until conditions are met  GMA News Online
articles.full_text:
DUBAI, United Arab Emirates - The Strait of Hormuz will not reopen until seven Iranian conditions set out in a June interim agreement with the US are met, state media reported Iran's parliament speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf as saying on Sunday.
Iran presented a proposal during the UN General Assembly under which the Strait of Hormuz waterway could be reopened and normal maritime passage restored within seven days if the conditions were met, with the US replying to this proposal last week via Qatari intermediaries.
"The position of the Islamic Republic of Iran is completely clear and firm, and the Strait of Hormuz will not be opened until our seven conditions, based on the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding, are met," Qalibaf, who is Iran's top negotiator, was quoted as saying.
He said Washington "must understand that the period of dragging out the (diplomatic) process and dictating one-sided demands is over".
Iran says no nuclear discussions
A Foreign Ministry spokesperson said on Sunday that Tehran had clarified its broad positions via mediators to the US response but that additional points remained to be communicated to Washington.
"The Americans' propositions are more or less in line with their previous positions, specifically on the nuclear issue. We told them our focus in this stage is the issue of the Strait of Hormuz and the return to security in this waterway requires clear steps from the US," spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said.
He also denied Tehran had offered UN nuclear watchdog inspections of its nuclear facilities in exchange for US sanctions relief, saying Iran had not entered into nuclear discussions with Washington.
The document being circulated outlines a seven-day period of trust-building aimed at returning the two sides to an enhanced version of the memorandum of understanding agreed in June, including concrete steps on Iran's nuclear program, an official briefed on the talks said last week.
The disagreement centers on the sequencing of the steps rather than the components of the plan, the official added.
Warning from Araqchi
Qatar has been shuttling messages between Washington and Tehran in an effort to end the conflict and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, the conduit for a fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas before the war that began at the end of February with US and Israeli attacks on Iran.
The June memorandum of understanding led to a brief ceasefire and included provisions on the strait and Iran's nuclear program.
Separately, Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi told foreign ambassadors and diplomats in Tehran on Sunday that Tehran hoped Washington would choose diplomacy but warned that Iran was prepared to respond if the US again chose military action.
On Thursday, sources told Reuters that Iran was preparing a broader and more forceful response if Washington resumed large-scale military attacks.
“If they again move towards military solutions, we are more prepared than before and will take whatever action is necessary to defend ourselves,” Araqchi said on Sunday.
Army spokesperson Mohammad Akraminia told Fars news agency on Sunday Iran would upgrade the range of its missiles. — Reuters

articles.title: Built to Be Announced, Not to Last: The Election Logic Behind a US–Iran Deal - Modern Diplomacy
articles.summary: Built to Be Announced, Not to Last: The Election Logic Behind a US–Iran Deal  Modern Diplomacy
articles.full_text:
Two Deadlines, One Date
Last Thursday, in Denton, Texas, Donald Trump said Iran is “ready to fold up” and that the war would be won “right after the election” — or “maybe before”. The same week he told TIME that new strikes after the vote were “possible”, and the Pentagon sent the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier group and the USS Makin Island amphibious group, about 9,000 sailors and Marines, towards the Gulf.
A week earlier, in New York, Iran’s president Masoud Pezeshkian had set the opposite deadline: “We don’t want it to get to the midterm elections.” Both governments have circled the same date, 3 November, and each believes the calendar favours it. That is the most important fact about these talks, and it points towards a deal built to be announced rather than one built to last.
Seven Days, Sixty Days, Three Weeks
The war began on 28 February. A memorandum of understanding signed on 17 June, mediated by Qatar and Pakistan, promised an end to fighting on all fronts, a lifted US naval blockade, mine clearance in Hormuz and a 60-day window for a wider deal. It lasted three weeks: a ship was struck on 25 June, the US retaliated on 27 June and Trump declared the agreement “over” on 7 July.
On 25 September foreign minister Abbas Araghchi offered a compressed version: a seven-day roadmap under which the US ends hostilities on all fronts, lifts the blockade, waives oil sanctions and releases at least $12 billion in frozen assets, with Hormuz reopening on day seven and nuclear talks to follow. Trump rejected it the next day but expects talks to resume. Both sides have since accepted the framework in principle; the gap, officials say, is the order of steps, not the steps themselves. Tehran, meanwhile, is hardening its public line: on 4 October parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said the strait will stay closed until Iran’s conditions are met.
Why the Clock Rewards a Thin Deal
Most coverage treats the election as background noise. It is the engine. Start with Washington. Gasoline is up about 52% since the war began, to roughly $4.48 a gallon; the Congressional Budget Office estimates the conflict has added 2.3 points to inflation; and Republican approval of the war has fallen from 73% in March to 60%, according to polling cited by TIME. Senate candidates in Iowa, Michigan and Ohio are now campaigning on ending it. Before 3 November, the president needs one thing above all: a visible fall in pump prices. That means Hormuz open, fast.
Tehran reads the same numbers and concludes that its leverage peaks now. Pezeshkian’s pre-election deadline is not goodwill; it is an attempt to sell a reopened strait at the highest price it will ever fetch. After the vote, Trump’s need for cheap fuel falls and his threats rise — he has said so on the record. Iran’s hardliners, who have filed impeachment motions against Araghchi over his meeting with US envoy Steve Witkoff, will tolerate a deal only if it looks like an American concession.
This is why the sequencing dispute is so stubborn. It is not a technicality; it is the election in diplomatic form. Washington wants Iran to move first, because a reopened strait lowers prices before voters go to the polls. Tehran wants money and sanctions waivers first, because once the strait is open its main bargaining chip is spent. Each side’s preferred order is set by the same date, which is why neither can give way on it without appearing to lose.
The likeliest way out is the one the June memorandum took: agree the headline steps — a ceasefire, a reopened strait, sanctions relief — and defer everything hard. That means the nuclear file, Israeli operations in Lebanon, Iran’s demand to control shipping routes through Hormuz, and the IRGC’s willingness to honour any of it. A deal of that shape can be announced in days. It also has no mechanism to survive the first incident at sea, which is exactly how the last one died.
The strongest objection is that deadlines are how diplomacy gets done, and a thin deal can thicken over time: the 2013 interim nuclear accord led to the 2015 agreement. But that accord rested on independent inspections that both sides valued keeping, and neither government was racing a vote. Here the enforcement tool is the strait itself, which Iran can close again at will, and the US calendar does not stop on 3 November: once the midterms pass, the political cost to Washington of walking away falls sharply. A deal timed to an election is a deal whose strongest supporter loses interest the day after it is signed.
The Pentagon seems to agree. Families of 82nd Airborne soldiers have been told some deployments could run into 2027, and the Theodore Roosevelt’s crew has been told to expect at least eight months at sea. Those are not the plans of an institution expecting peace by Thanksgiving.
Three Endings
Base case — an announced deal that frays (about 45%). A framework is agreed either just before or within weeks of 3 November: ceasefire, phased reopening of Hormuz, oil-sanctions waivers and partial release of frozen funds, with nuclear and Lebanon questions pushed into a follow-on negotiation. Oil falls sharply on the news. Within three to six months a strike on a vessel, a dispute over shipping routes or an Israeli operation in Lebanon reopens the fight. For business, this means treating any early relief in freight and fuel prices as temporary. Expect the announcement to be framed around tanker traffic, not nuclear terms — that framing is the tell.
Downside — no deal, then escalation (about 35%). Talks stall over sequencing until the vote. Freed from electoral pressure, Trump orders the strikes he has called “possible”; Iran answers through the Houthis and the Red Sea rather than directly, the route that matters most to Riyadh, as MD has argued, now that the Red Sea, not Hormuz, decides Saudi foreign policy. The closure runs into 2027 and the second carrier group stays.
Upside — a deal built on verification, not dates (about 20%). Qatar and Pakistan, with Oman on shipping routes, broker a deal sequenced by verifiable steps — IAEA access, route arrangements in the strait, staged release of funds — and implemented over months rather than days. That requires both sides to give up the election as a deadline, which is why it is the least likely outcome and the only durable one. The signal would be Oman, not just Qatar, named as a party to the text.
A Deal for November, Not for 2027
Both capitals have bet on the same date, from opposite directions. The bet makes an agreement more likely in the next month, and makes it worse. A deal designed to be announced before or just after 3 November will be strong on headlines and weak on enforcement, and its main backer will have less reason to defend it once the votes are counted. As Iran’s own strategic calculus suggests, Tehran will not give up its hold on Hormuz in a hurry.
Watch for Iran’s formal reply to the US response, expected once its internal review ends, and check one thing in any text that follows: whether it names who verifies Iran’s steps and who controls shipping routes through the strait. If it names neither, it is a ceasefire with a press release attached — and it will last about as long as the last one.

Israeli strike kills 1 in central Gaza, local health officials say
An Israeli strike Sunday morning on a civilian vehicle killed one Palestinian and wounded at least 11 others, according to health officials at the Aqsa Martyrs Hospital, where the casualties were taken.
Israel’s military said it targeted a known Hamas militant in the strike.
Palestinians in Gaza have reported a surge in Israeli fire and airstrikes across the enclave over the past month. Israel says it is targeting Hamas and other militants who pose a threat, and in response to ceasefire violations, including occasional attacks.
Israeli strikes have killed at least 1,445 Palestinians in Gaza since a ceasefire was reached with the Hamas militant group nearly a year ago, according to the territory’s Health Ministry. Its figures are seen as generally reliable by U.N. agencies and independent experts. It doesn’t give a breakdown of civilians and militants. Seven Israeli soldiers have been killed in Gaza since the ceasefire.
Houthis say midnight airstrike hits Yemeni capital
The Iranian-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen said airstrikes hit the capital, Sanaa, at midnight amid their renewed war against Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government.
The Houthi media office reported the strikes without giving further details. It accused Saudi Arabia of launching the strikes, but didn’t offer evidence and there was no immediate comment from Saudi Arabia.
However, the Yemeni military, which is backed by Riyadh, claimed responsibility for the strikes.
Yemeni military spokesman Col. Majed al-Nazili said it struck “vital targets” in Sanaa as well as the northern province of Saada on the borders with Saudi Arabia.
Airstrikes that hit Sanaa on Saturday morning were also claimed by the Yemeni military.
The attacks were part of a major escalation between Saudi Arabia and the Iranian-backed Houthis that revived Yemen’s civil war after a four-year ceasefire.
Tanker in Strait of Hormuz struck by projectile, British military says
A projectile struck a tanker on the Strait of Hormuz Sunday, damaging the engine room, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Center said.
It was not immediately clear who launched the attack, nor was it clear when it was carried out. The UKMTO said the crew was reportedly safe.
Overall ship traffic remains below prewar levels in the Strait of Hormuz, as do shipments of energy products, even though Iran has lost its near-complete chokehold over the crucial waterway due to the U.S. Navy’s efforts to shepherd oil tankers through the strait. That, along with various pipelines, has allowed Gulf countries to restore oil exports to nearly prewar levels.

Israeli embassies in the United States and the United Kingdom are promoting a copycat NAZA, nearly a month after the release of the original that focuses on testimony of Israelis killing Palestinians in Gaza.
In posts on X, the embassies said that "Naza: The Real Story" is "setting the record straight" and claims to offer a firsthand account from senior Israeli military commanders and intelligence officers directly involved in Israel's genocidal war on Gaza.
It said the film uses combat footage, declassified materials, captured intelligence and firsthand testimony to give context on "how the war was fought and the challenges Israeli forces faced".
The film's website names the provider as Three Musketeers Production, "a company in formation", and says a registered address and registration number will be published once the company is registered. It says the directors are deliberately not named "for their safety".
Claimed to have been filmed on the rooftops of Tel Aviv, the 49-minute documentary is available in 17 languages on its official website.
"Rooftop interviews with senior IDF [Israeli army] commanders: Hamas fighters in civilian clothes, hostages held in homes, aid and Hamas. For people about to watch this film, not a NASA picture," reads a blog entry about the film.
The website lists a release date of 20 September 2026 and says the film will also be shown in theatres.
Blog posts on the film's website, dated 18-26 September, summarise interviews it says are included in the documentary.
"One interview covers Gaza from north to south. No personal names appear on this page, and the directors are unnamed for security reasons," the website notes.
"This page summarises what the interviewee says. It reports his account and the IDF rules he describes. It does not verify them independently."
'Hang the traitors'
Directed by Israeli journalists Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, NAZA: A Window into Systems of Mass Killing has riled the Israeli government and far-right elements of Israeli society since its premiere and Special Jury Prize win at the Venice International Film Festival last month.
The 25-minute standing ovation for the film set a new record for any movie at a major festival, surpassing the near 24 minutes by The Voice of Hind Rajab at last year's Venice festival.
NAZA examines the AI-powered systems used in Israel's war on Gaza and allegations that high numbers of Palestinian civilian deaths were factored into military targeting decisions.
The documentary features interviews with 24 Israeli military and intelligence insiders, whose identities remained anonymous.
Israeli politicians, journalists and members of the public have attacked Szor and Abraham, accusing them of treason and calling for their citizenship to be revoked.
Last month, Culture Minister Miki Zohar called the film "despicable" and said he would "act immediately to revoke the Israeli citizenship of these despicable creators on the grounds of treason against the state".
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu joined Zohar in attacking the filmmakers, saying he would introduce two bills targeting those who "defame" the Israeli military.
Netanyahu said the first bill "would revoke the citizenship of anyone who defames soldiers", while the second would increase "twentyfold the amount in damages for which they can be sued for defamation".
"They have no place among us," Netanyahu said of those who "defame" the Israeli army.
The Israeli military's Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir has ordered legal action against Szor and Abraham with the help of the Shin Bet, according to Israeli media.
Dozens of far-right Israelis gathered outside Szor's family home on 16 September, demanding she be hanged.
The Israeli newspaper Haaretz reported that several of the protesters demanded the "death penalty for traitors".
One demonstrator said that when Szor and Abraham return to Israel, "they should be tried and go to the gallows, and the family should be expelled and the house sealed".
Many social media users dismissed the documentary as "propaganda" and an attempt to "bury the real film".
An X account named Britain United wrote: "Pathetic, that actual Naza documentary must be really exposing for you to try to SEO bury the real film online by using the same title."
"You can try and spin the Israeli slaughter of the residents of Gaza all you want, but it won't work," X user Joe said.

South Asian energy planners are seeking equity partnerships with Middle Eastern sovereign funds to finance a major expansion of India’s downstream oil processing infrastructure.
Last month, Indian Minister of Petroleum and Natural Gas Hardeep Singh Puri stated that major regional energy producers, including Saudi Arabia and the UAE, have expressed strong interest in funding projects within the nation’s refining sector.
The initiative supports India’s plan to increase national refining capacity from 5.4mn barrels per day (bpd) to over 6.2mn bpd to meet rising domestic fuel requirements.
Alongside direct refining proposals from regional peers, India is broadening its diplomatic outreach to Qatar to secure institutional capital across the broader energy value chain.
In April 2026, during a two-day official visit to Doha, Puri met Minister of State for Energy Affairs His Excellency Saad Sherida al-Kaabi, who is also president and CEO of QatarEnergy, to discuss strategic relations, trade, investment, and maritime supply chain security.
During the meeting, both officials reaffirmed bilateral energy cooperation while stressing the necessity of maintaining stability in global fuel supplies and ensuring unhindered maritime commerce during regional disruptions, according to state-run Qatar News Agency (QNA).
While trade between the two nations has historically been anchored by long-term liquefied natural gas (LNG) supply agreements, bilateral dialogue is increasingly focusing on mutual equity participation in processing assets, the website of the Indian Embassy in Qatar stated.
Long-term gas trade remains a central pillar, highlighted by Petronet LNG’s 20-year contract extension in 2024 to purchase 7.5mn tonnes of LNG annually from QatarEnergy through July 2028 and beyond, QNA also reported.
To facilitate structured financial flows into new sectors, India and Qatar established the Joint Task Force on Investment (JTFI) to explore commercial opportunities across infrastructure, technology, and energy.
The inaugural meeting of the joint working group took place in New Delhi in June 2024, co-chaired by Ministry of Commerce and Industry Undersecretary Mohammed bin Hassan al-Maliki and India’s Department of Economic Affairs Undersecretary Ajay Seth.
During the meeting, al-Maliki highlighted that bilateral trade volume reached approximately $13.46bn in 2023, positioning India as Qatar’s second-largest trading partner.
At the time, Qatari exports to India consist primarily of LNG, liquefied petroleum gas, chemicals, petrochemicals, plastics, and aluminium products. Indian exports to Qatar include cereals, copper articles, iron and steel products, vegetables, spices, electrical machinery, construction materials, and manufactured textiles, it was reported.
Bilateral economic interaction is further supported by formal financial frameworks, including a Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement (DTAA) signed in April 1999 that came into effect in January 2000 to prevent fiscal evasion and govern income tax rates.
Under the agreement, specific withholding tax rates are set at 10% for interest, royalties, and technical service fees, while dividend withholding tax is set at 5% for corporate holdings of at least 10%.
The institutional framework builds upon a proven track record of Qatari sovereign wealth deployment in Indian utility and power infrastructure assets. The Qatar Investment Authority (QIA) acquired a 25.1% stake in Adani Electricity Mumbai Limited (AEML) in February 2020 for approximately $450mn, establishing an initial operational presence in urban power distribution.
In August 2023, QIA expanded its energy portfolio by acquiring a 2.68% equity stake in Adani Green Energy Limited (AGEL) for approximately $500mn through its subsidiary INQ Holding.
QNA reported that in April this year, Qatar Central Bank Governor His Excellency Sheikh Bandar bin Mohammed bin Saoud al-Thani, who is also chairman of QIA, held a meeting with AGEL executive director Sagar Adani, where they discussed the latest developments in global finance and investment.
According to official reports, India is expected to drive 25% of global energy demand growth over the next two decades, prompting the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas to target sovereign wealth partnerships for refining capital and fuel security.

articles.title: Iran’s terrifying new terror tactic may be turning airline pilots into 9/11-style attackers, former IDF colonel warns - New York Post

articles.full_text:
The hijacking of the Dubai airliner carrying Israeli passengers might be the beginning of a horrifying new terrorist tactic of recruiting and radicalizing real pilots to do 9/11-style attacks, a former IDF colonel and veteran intelligence officer warns.
“An individual doesn’t get the idea on his own to crash a plane full of people including himself. Somebody told him that if you do that you get your 72 virgins,” Miri Eisin, now an Israeli government spokesman, told The Post.
“If you think back to past plane hijackings, including 9/11, the hijacker was never the pilot of the plane. . . . This could be a new kind of suicide bomber,” she said.
Eisin, who served in the Israel Defense Forces as an intelligence officer for over 20 years, said she immediately suspected Iran’s hand in the near-tragic FlyDubai hijacking — though she was careful to stress she has no direct evidence and that the investigation is ongoing.
She said that the Omani pilot who stabbed his Indian co-pilot and attempted to crash the plane full of 174 passengers before he was overpowered by heroic Israeli passengers could have been radicalized by the Islamic Republic or its terrorist proxies.
President Trump has also suggested Iran might have been involved, but did not elaborate.
The pilot has been identified by The Wall Street Journal as an Omani national named Hamam al-Hammami. He had previously been banned from flying by Oman due to suspicions he had become radicalized, according to the publication.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said that the attacker had been subject to “Islamic radicalization.”
“This to me is very much something that could have come from Hezbollah or the IRGC Quds Force, this is the kind of things that they think of,” she said.
Eisin said that Iran, if responsible for the attack, may be trying to unleash a new kind of suicide bomber by infiltrating airlines with radicalized pilots who could launch an attack at any time.
Eisin said a pilot’s professional training would not make him immune to extremist indoctrination.
“Just because someone’s a pilot doesn’t mean they can’t be radicalized, people from all walks of life could be radicalized. [Syrian dictator] Bashar al-Assad was a doctor, Josef Mengele was a doctor,” she said.
“And if you kill Israelis, the whole world applauds you,” she added.
Oded Ailam, a former deputy head of global operations for Israel’s Mossad intelligence agency, said recruiting a commercial pilot to deliberately crash a plane would require a far more elaborate process than persuading a young suicide bomber to carry out an attack.
“Recruiting and convincing a pilot to do something like that, it’s not the same as telling a 15-year-old to strap on a bomb and walk into a promenade and explode himself. This is a very sophisticated and long operation,” he said.
Ailam, who is now a researcher at the Jerusalem Center for Security and Foreign Affairs, said that it’s likely that Iran was able to radicalize the pilot passively without formally recruiting him via its vast array of anti-Israel propaganda online and in other venues.
“The lone wolf is influenced by the pack of wolves around him, he’s influenced by jihadists, by extremists in mosques, he’s influenced by prominent Iranians calling for death to Israel,” he said.
Ailam said that the prospect of lone wolf extremists could pose an even more dangerous threat to air travel than organized terror cells that could be identified and disrupted.
“Terror combined with mental disturbances in the pilot, when you combine it together the outcome is horrific. There are a lot of people who are being radicalized who are airline pilots,” he said.
Ailam said the flydubai attack will likely lead governments to rethink their post-9/11 security measures, and he predicts airlines will soon have to install technology that lets crew access the cockpit in the case of a copycat attack.
“It’s impossible to screen every pilot, the answer will have to be technological,” he said.

articles.title: Pakistan’s LNG Paradox: When An Energy Fix Became An Economic Liability - The Friday Times
articles.summary: Pakistan’s LNG Paradox: When An Energy Fix Became An Economic Liability  The Friday Times
articles.full_text:
Pakistan’s energy economy is caught in an unusual contradiction. On one hand, the country has had more liquefied natural gas (LNG) than it could use, forcing it to divert contracted cargoes to other markets. On the other, when the 2026 Middle East conflict disrupted LNG supplies, Pakistan had to worry about shortages and look again towards the expensive global spot market. At the same time, the gas sector’s circular debt has reached around Rs3.3 trillion, with the costs eventually spreading across the wider economy through higher energy prices, pressure on public finances and losses within state-owned companies.
So how did a fuel once introduced as part of the solution to Pakistan’s energy crisis become such a significant economic burden?
A new report offers an important starting point. On October 1, 2026, Recourse, Africa Change Lab and The Big Shift Global released Gas Is Bad Economics for the Global South, examining the economics of fossil gas in five developing countries, including Pakistan. Its central argument is that countries investing heavily in gas as a “bridge fuel” towards cleaner energy can become locked into debt, volatile international prices and infrastructure that may become less useful as energy markets change. Pakistan provides an important case study of that argument.
A Solution For A Time Of Shortage
Between 2014 and 2016, Pakistan developed infrastructure and long-term arrangements to import LNG. There was a clear reason for doing so. Domestic gas production was declining, industries were struggling with shortages, and prolonged power cuts were hurting businesses and households. Imported LNG offered a relatively quick way to supply fuel to power plants, reduce dependence on expensive furnace oil and provide gas to industry. But the underlying challenge was and remains — energy access. For households and businesses, access means more than having an electricity or gas connection. Energy must also be reliable and affordable. An imported-fuel system therefore cannot be judged only by how much energy it brings into the country, but also by whether its costs help expand affordable and dependable access.
It would be unfair to judge decisions made a decade ago entirely with the benefit of hindsight. Policymakers in 2015 could not have known how quickly solar technology would become cheaper or precisely how Pakistan’s electricity demand would change. The more important question is whether the country’s long-term energy arrangements were flexible enough to adapt when prices, technology and demand changed. Today, that question is worth billions of dollars.
A March 2026 study by the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis (IEEFA) found that Pakistan had to make arrangements to divert about 45 surplus LNG cargoes contracted from Qatar and Italy’s ENI to other markets. Based on projections by Pakistan’s Petroleum Division, IEEFA estimates that, if the mismatch between demand and contracted supply is not addressed, Pakistan could face as many as 177 surplus cargoes through 2032, with a potential liability of about $5.6 billion, or more if oil prices rise. This is a projection of financial risk rather than a loss Pakistan has already incurred, but it illustrates how expensive long-term contracts can become when the assumptions behind them change.
Then Came The Solar Revolution
While Pakistan remained tied to long-term gas arrangements, consumers were changing the energy market themselves. As grid electricity became more expensive and solar panels became cheaper, households, shops, factories and farmers increasingly began producing their own electricity. IEEFA estimates that Pakistan’s distributed solar capacity reached around 34 gigawatts in 2025, including grid-connected and off-grid systems. Meanwhile, electricity demand from the national grid in fiscal year 2025 was almost 11 per cent lower than in fiscal year 2022. Solar was not the only factor: high electricity prices, weaker industrial demand and slow economic growth also contributed. But solar has clearly become an important part of Pakistan’s changing electricity market.
The change has reached the gas market. Pakistan’s LNG consumption fell by around 1.21 million tonnes in 2025. According to IEEFA, LNG-based electricity generation declined by about 4.5 terawatt-hours, while industrial gas demand also weakened. This creates a difficult economic situation. Consumers reduce their dependence on expensive grid electricity by installing solar panels, lowering demand for some gas-fired generation. The country consequently needs less imported gas. Yet long-term LNG contracts do not automatically adjust when demand falls. Pakistan’s contracts have included “take-or-pay” commitments, under which buyers carry payment obligations for contracted supplies even when demand is weaker, subject to the flexibility provisions of individual agreements. Such arrangements can provide supply security when demand is high, but they reduce flexibility when consumption falls unexpectedly. Pakistan’s LNG surplus therefore exposes a fundamental mismatch: energy demand can change much faster than long-term contractual commitments.
How Can Pakistan Have Too Much Gas And Too Little?
The contradiction became even clearer during the 2026 Middle East conflict. Before the crisis, Pakistan was trying to manage surplus LNG. When regional supply routes were disrupted, however, the country suddenly faced another problem: securing enough gas during periods of high demand. Pakistan introduced an emergency gas management plan and again had to consider buying LNG from the international spot market.
Solar power and a more diverse electricity mix helped the national grid cope with reduced LNG availability. But solar does not produce electricity at night, meaning gas and other dependable sources were still required to meet peak evening demand. This highlights an important aspect of energy security. It is not simply about signing contracts to buy more fuel. Pakistan has long-term LNG contracts but very limited capacity to store LNG. When demand is low, surplus gas creates pressure on the system; when international supply is suddenly disrupted, the same country can face shortages. Surplus and shortage are therefore not necessarily opposites. In Pakistan’s case, they can be two symptoms of the same problem: an energy system that does not have enough flexibility.
When Imported Gas Pushed Out Cheaper Local Gas
Perhaps one of the most striking examples came in 2025. Pakistan had too much gas in its pipeline system and insufficient storage capacity, causing pipeline pressure to rise. To manage the problem, the government had to reduce production from domestic gas fields by around 270 to 400 million cubic feet per day. IEEFA reports that state-owned Oil and Gas Development Company suffered around Rs43 billion in revenue losses as a result.
The economics are difficult to ignore. According to the IEEFA analysis, imported LNG was roughly three times as expensive as domestic gas. Yet contractual obligations and limited storage meant that, at times, Pakistan had to reduce production of cheaper domestic gas while imported LNG remained in the system. At that point, the problem was no longer simply the international price of LNG. The structure of the system itself was creating additional costs.
 Pakistan’s LNG surplus and recurring gas shortages are not necessarily opposites; they can be two symptoms of the same problem — an energy system that lacks the flexibility to respond to changing demand and supply.
The Rs3.3 Trillion Question
Pakistan’s gas-sector circular debt adds another layer to the problem. By early 2026, it stood at around Rs3.3 trillion. It would be wrong to attribute all of this debt to LNG. The problem has multiple causes, including differences between the actual cost of gas and prices charged to some consumers, subsidies, unpaid bills, old liabilities, theft, pipeline leakage and problems with measurement and recovery. But expensive imported gas makes these weaknesses more costly. IEEFA estimates that unaccounted-for gas losses are around 11.7 per cent. This can include technical leakage, theft, metering problems and other losses. Not all of this can simply be described as poor management, since gas networks inevitably experience some technical losses. Nevertheless, reducing leakage, controlling theft, improving metering and recovering bills remain basic responsibilities of gas companies and regulators.
This matters directly to ordinary consumers. If Pakistan imports expensive gas, fails to recover all its costs, loses a significant amount within the system and then responds by increasing tariffs, consumers are not paying only for the international price of gas. They can also end up carrying part of the cost of weaknesses within the domestic system. The government therefore needs to distinguish between the different sources of the financial gap: imported fuel, subsidies, unpaid bills, old liabilities and losses within gas companies. Without that separation, higher tariffs risk becoming a substitute for better management.
The Role Of International Finance
Pakistan’s LNG system was not built with domestic resources alone. International financial institutions helped finance parts of the infrastructure. The International Finance Corporation and the Asian Development Bank participated in financing Pakistan’s first major LNG terminal, while other institutions supported gas transmission, energy-sector reforms and fuel imports. At the time, the logic was understandable. Pakistan urgently needed energy, and LNG appeared to offer a faster alternative to shortages and expensive liquid fuels. But development finance cannot be judged only by whether a project was successfully built. Energy markets, technology and demand change, and the long-term economics of earlier investments need to be reassessed when they do.

Senior Iranian military and security officials have been photographed wearing smartwatches, drawing fresh criticism of their basic security discipline after years of reports that Israel has used electronic devices around Iranian commanders to track and kill them.
The images drew widespread reactions after they were posted on X on Friday by Ali Gholhaki, a conservative commentator with ties to Iran's security establishment. Some Iranian outlets describe him as close to parliament speaker Mohammad-Bagher Ghalibaf.
The pictures show smartwatches on the wrists of three men: Gholamreza Jalali, who heads the Passive Defense Organization, the body that protects Iran's critical infrastructure; Reza Farahi, a Defense Ministry official; and Ali Shamkhani, the former secretary of the Supreme National Security Council.
Shamkhani was killed in US-Israeli airstrikes on February 28, on the first day of the current war. He had survived an Israeli strike in June 2025.
Asked about his watch by a Fars News reporter, Jalali asked whether people had smart televisions at home and said his device was effectively the same thing.
Gholhaki rejected the comparison. The man in charge of protecting the country's critical infrastructure, he argued, faces a different order of risk from an ordinary citizen, and such devices are hard to justify for senior security officials when Israel has repeatedly exploited electronic lapses to track Iranian personnel.

Smartwatches can transmit location and activity data through GPS, Bluetooth, Wi-Fi or a paired phone, and some carry microphones and other sensors.
The US military has long restricted location-tracking devices, smartwatches included, in operational areas because they can expose movements and routines; in 2018, a fitness app's public heat map revealed the outlines of American bases from soldiers' running routes.
'Careless use'
The row touches a much larger argument inside the Islamic Republic about repeated intelligence failures.
During the 12-day war in June 2025, Iran's Cyber Security Command banned officials and their security teams from using any device connected to public communication or telecommunications networks, Fars reported, as concern grew that mobile tracking was being used for targeted assassinations.
The directive named smartphones, laptops and smartwatches, and warned that switching a device off might not prevent it from being located.
It came too late. The New York Times later reported, citing Iranian and Israeli officials, that Israel tracked and targeted senior Iranian leaders and nuclear scientists in that war by hacking the phones of their bodyguards and drivers.
On June 16, 2025, the Supreme National Security Council met in a bunker deep beneath a mountain in western Tehran; none of the officials carried phones, but the Israelis found the meeting through the phones of the bodyguards who had driven them there. The bodyguards had long been exempt from the strict phone bans imposed on the commanders themselves, even after earlier assassinations.
Gholhaki tied the smartwatches directly to those failures, arguing that complacency had helped Israel and the United States kill senior military, security and political figures in successive wars. He called for fundamental changes in security practice and renewed his demand for a broad postwar inquiry into how the failures happened.
Gholhaki himself was among a group of Telegram channel operators arrested by the Revolutionary Guards' counterintelligence arm in 2022, accused of disturbing public opinion and publishing classified documents.
A blogger on death row
The judiciary has shown no such tolerance for ordinary Iranians accused of far smaller breaches.
Marziyeh "Sevda" Ebrahimi Shamsabadi, a 33-year-old blogger from Bandar Abbas who has been held since March, was sentenced to death in August by a Revolutionary Court on charges including insulting the supreme leader, intelligence activity on behalf of hostile governments, and taking and sending photographs to Persian-language media abroad.
One allegation concerned a photograph she was said to have taken, from a distance, of a site hit by a missile. She was held in solitary confinement for 20 days and faced severe pressure during interrogation.

Ukraine will double down on attacking Russian oil refineries in response to a new policy of airstrikes by Moscow designed to force people to abandon Kyiv and other cities, but will not target civilians, President Volodymyr Zelensky said.
Ukrainian intelligence has obtained documents showing that Russian leader Vladimir Putin had issued a “new doctrine” of military attacks on a much broader range of civilian targets ahead of winter, Zelensky said.
“We saw documents and we know that they allow them to attack infrastructure ... logistics ... roads, schools, hospitals, to pressure people to leave the capital, leave different cities,” Zelensky said. “This is the goal of the operation.”
Driving the shift in policy, Zelensky said, was Putin's desire to appear strong at a time when his military was losing ground in a key frontline region and sustaining higher levels of casualties.
The Kremlin was not available to comment on Saturday. But in a statement urging foreign nationals to leave Kyiv, the Russian Foreign Ministry said Moscow would continue to systematically hit targets in what it said were retaliatory strikes for Ukrainian attacks on Russia in recent months.
Both sides deny deliberately targeting civilians.
Counteroffensive in Donbas
Zelensky said an ongoing Ukrainian counteroffensive, code-named “Vivaldi,” had recaptured around 140 sq km (54 sq miles) of Ukraine's eastern Donbas region, which Russia has said it must control in its entirety as a condition for any peace deal.
In recent weeks, U.S. President Donald Trump's administration has sought to revive talks to end the four-year-old conflict — Europe's bloodiest since World War Two.
The U.S. leader last month urged Ukraine to refrain from hitting Russian oil installations, saying that was sending global diesel prices surging.
But Zelensky, speaking as air raid sirens blared outside the gilded halls of the presidential offices, said he had received no indications from Russia that Putin was interested in peace talks or discussing a ceasefire on energy infrastructure.
Over the past week, the Ukrainian capital has come under persistent attack by Russian drones and missiles targeting energy and telecoms assets, road and rail infrastructure. For the first time, Russia has targeted the bridges across the Dnipro River connecting east and west Kyiv.
Zelensky said Ukraine would respond to the change in tactics by Moscow, but would not respond in kind by targeting civilian infrastructure indiscriminately.
“We have to respond in any way (we can). With their attacks on our energy, we have to respond on their energy. First of all, oil refiners: what gives money to them for this war,” Zelensky said in English. “But we will not respond, of course, just like them, on any civilian objects.”
Support from Europe
After the Trump administration invited Putin to attend a G20 summit in Miami in December and discussed business deals with Russian envoys, Zelensky urged Washington not to normalise relations with Russia before ensuring a return to peace.
Zelensky said he would be happy to meet Putin for peace talks at the G20, but he warned the U.S. not to believe in “illusions” that Russia would end hostilities if it gained control of Donbas.
“It's not fair just to normalize,” said Zelensky, dressed in his trademark black T-shirt and military-style jacket. Any resumption of economic and diplomatic ties with the West had to be in return for peace, he said: “Because peace is more important than any kind of economy.”
While the U.S. has proposed resuming trilateral talks in the coming weeks in the UAE, Zelensky noted that an exact date and location for the technical-level conversations had not been set.
Ukrainian officials warn that Russia has stockpiled hundreds of ballistic missiles ahead of an expected winter onslaught against electricity and water infrastructure. Last winter, the worst of the war, Russian strikes left swathes of the country without electricity and heating for days at a time.
Since the summer, Moscow has also begun launching dozens of fast and relatively cheap jet-powered Shahed drones a day at Ukraine, whose air defenses have struggled as its previous generation of interceptor drones are too slow to catch them.
Zelensky said Ukraine had been forced to rely heavily on its fighter aircraft — F-16s and MiGs — to down around 60% of the Russian jet-powered drones, but supplies of 20 mm ammunition for the planes were running low.
Kyiv was urgently working on other solutions — including boosting its jamming capabilities, he said. In the second half of October, it should receive its first shipment of small, cheap air defense missiles capable of hitting the new Shaheds.
Last week, Zelensky said Ukraine was developing five models of new interceptor drones capable of downing the jet Shaheds. Fresh from a meeting with his defense chiefs, he said tests on two of those models showed a modest success rate of around 30%.
“We'll have to scale it,” he said. “I hope that with all these things, with all these elements, we'll find a way.”
Ballistic threat
Ukraine announced the first combat use this week of its own domestically made ballistic missile — the FP-7, which has a range of around 250 km (155 miles).
Zelensky said he had called the manufacturer Fire Point to pressure executives to quickly finish a longer-range model, the FP-9, which the company has said could hit Moscow.
“I said to them, ‘Where is my FP-9?’” said Zelensky, with a grin. “We need the FP-9. And the FP-9 will be (ready) this autumn, I'm sure.”
Zelensky said a recent spate of Russian drone incursions and hybrid attacks in Europe were an effort to intimidate European populations and to divide support for Ukraine.
Some European leaders were starting to understand this, he said, and toughen their position.
Russia says such accusations are baseless and the result of anti-Russian hysteria.
After talks with European officials in Brussels this week, Ukraine found funding to proceed with orders for drones that it needs to keep fighting at the start of 2027, Zelensky said.
Ukrainian officials had worked on a plan with European partners to plug a $27 billion hole in Kyiv's defense budget this year.
The plans involve a combination of the reallocation of Ukraine's own budget resources, bilateral assistance, and using “money credits” from next year's portion of a €90 billion EU loan, Zelensky said.

articles.title: War-displaced Gazans fear another winter without shelter, aid
articles.summary: Gaza's war-displaced population faces yet another winter with little to no shelter and dwindling aid due to Israeli stranglehold on the Palestinian territory. Displaced people in t...
articles.full_text:
Gaza's war-displaced population faces yet another winter with little to no shelter and dwindling aid due to Israeli stranglehold on the Palestinian territory.
Displaced people in the southern Gaza Strip appealed Saturday for tents, blankets and basic supplies ahead of winter.
They warned that shelter shortages and dwindling humanitarian aid could leave thousands exposed to rain, cold and strong winds.
Dozens of displaced residents staged a protest in the Fash Farsh area in Khan Younis, urging international organizations and donors to provide shelter materials, food and essential supplies amid Israel’s blockade.
"Our tents are torn and our stomachs are empty. Do not leave us to the unknown," read one of the signs by protesters.
Families said they fear a repeat of previous winters, when heavy rains flooded and damaged tents, leaving them exposed to harsh weather.
Deaths, including mostly children, were also reported during periods of severe cold and after damaged buildings collapsed.
"We are heading into winter and we need tarpaulins, tents, food and health supplies so we can withstand the heavy rain and winds," Iyad Zomor told Turkish Anadolu Agency (AA).
Iyad al-Shaer said many tents offered little protection from cold, rain or wind, urging humanitarian organizations to provide shelter materials before weather conditions worsen.
Ahmed Hassan al-Najjar, who oversees Fash Farsh, told AA that 35 displacement camps there shelter 6,000 families, or about 40,000 people.
He said residents were facing shortages of tents, tarpaulins, food parcels and medical supplies and called for urgent assistance.
Israel's genocidal war in Gaza has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and injured over 175,000 in Gaza since October 2023, while 90% of the enclave’s infrastructure has been reduced to rubble.
